comparisons.apparatus_caveat: Each complete declared constituent has its own source boundaries and normalization; neither is a complete Ordinary or Missal. The 1657 extent includes its final Secreta/preface posture rubric; the 1606 extent ends with the Dominus sit response. Printing dates do not establish first introduction of every change. Institutional revision does not establish direct descent between these exact copies; both native versions have no Git parents or text inheritance. The earlier selected-prayer comparisons retain their narrower scope.
comparisons.basis: Complete source-bounded offertory constituents within the 1606 Præparationes ante Missam and 1657 Ordo Missæ. The 1606 combined paten/chalice offering is compared with the 1657 separate offerings, water prayer, incense prayers, Lavabo and later Suscipe Trinitas. All included rubrics and response cues retain their source order. This aligns a liturgical function, rather than identifying every prayer as the same composition.

comparisons.apparatus_caveat: The 1606 extent is printed sequence 190–197 (the fourth page is misnumbered 192); the 1657 extent is discontiguous proper-form blocks on printed 176, 177, 181, 183, 184 plus the Canon title and main 203–213, ending before Oremus/Pater. Other preface texts and all other book divisions are excluded. Different physical placement does not establish abolition of the seasonal forms. Source spelling, accents, punctuation and rubric segmentation retain their declared normalizations; unequal unit counts do not establish substantive ritual revision or an introduction date. Both native Canon versions remain parentless: Roman reception and institutional revision do not yet identify the exact predecessor textual states. No whole-book completeness or text inheritance is claimed.
comparisons.basis: Complete declared Canon constituents in the independently collated 1606 and 1657 witnesses. The 1606 strict Canon span contains its five seasonal Communicantes forms and Easter/Pentecost Hanc igitur; the 1657 selection includes five Communicantes and two separately printed Hanc igitur forms, their headings and governing cues from the preceding preface section, followed by the main Canon. Each side retains its own physical source order and complete declared wording, including rubrics. This aligns a liturgical function without treating every rubric or paragraph division as the same composition.

comparisons.apparatus_caveat: The left selection is printed p. 197 after and excluding the prior strict-Canon final Amen, ending at the post-Pater Amen before Libera. The right selection is FIDES raw 0275 right / printed p. 213 from Oremus, then raw 0276 / printed p. 214 through the FIRST Amen, before the Sequens cantus rubric. The second 1657 chant and its governing rubric, Per omnia/Amen, repeated introduction, prayer and terminal Amen remain in the native binding but are excluded from this comparison. The following Sequens cantus rubric is cited only as contextual evidence for that exclusion; it assigns the second form to three-lesson feasts, ferial days and Masses for the dead, and does not by itself establish an exclusive usage rule for the first form. The wider untranscribed 1657 post-Canon continuation is outside scope, so this comparison makes no claim that its prayers were absent. Source punctuation, accents, display-initial case, cœ/cæ ligatures and the interleaved rubric positions retain each artifact’s declared normalization; the literal text diff is not a comparison of chant pitches. The worn/creased final Amén reading belongs to the excluded second form, not the selected first Amen. Publication dates identify these witnesses, not the introduction of any wording or rubric. No whole-book completeness, historical descent, act, inherited wording or date of change is inferred.
comparisons.basis: Complete Pater noster invitation, prayer, Sed libera response and final Amen in the Paris 1606 Cistercian witness, aligned with the first of the two printed 1657 chant forms. The incipit, full petition sequence and response establish witnesses of the same prayer. Six maintained 1606 units correspond to three maintained 1657 units; the latter retain Extendit manus inside the introduction and Sacerdos secretè dicit before Amen. Each side preserves its exact source order, wording and governing rubrics; unequal unit counts do not imply unequal prayer extent.

source_record.note: Original acquired from ULB Bonn (Goussen 1665). Propaganda Fide pro negotiis Ritus Orientalis approved the book on 25 February 1913 as revised and purged of errors, for priests of the rite received in Abyssinia; the Vicar Apostolic of Eritrea, C. Carrara, gave the imprimatur at Asmara on 12 April 1913. The title-page imprint reads ፲፱፻፯, equated with 1914/15 by Hammerschmidt and the Encyclopaedia Aethiopica. Section headings show the Apostles anaphora, an order of Communion and anaphoras numbered 2 to 14 (Our Lord; Mary; John son of Thunder; 318 Orthodox; Athanasius; Basil; Gregory of Nyssa; Epiphanius; John Chrysostom; Cyril; Dionysius; a heading for Däbrä Zäyt and Ṗagʷəmen; Gregory of Armenia), consistent with the Keren studies' count of fourteen. The New Catholic Encyclopedia reports Carrara sought to reprint the 1890 missal; the approbation's wording claims revision, so whole-book identity with 1890 is not established. source_record.limitations: Exact title, holding copy, decree and page loci remain missing. No claim that 2025 retains these changes.
source_record.note: Seventeen-anaphora Catholic edition. Bishop Kidane Yebio identifies it as the source of a literal Blin translation, establishing bounded Eritrean reception. A Keren 2009 Tigrinya study compares a specific Spirit invocation across 1890, 1913 and 1945 and lists three added anaphoras; the table does not mean earlier books lacked every epiclesis. The publisher’s signed 2024 note explicitly says the new edition replaces 1945. Exact original 1945 pages and editorial decree remain unacquired. The Encyclopaedia Aethiopica (mirror) says the Vatican press prepared it under Arnold van Lantschoot to correct earlier editions and lists 17 anaphoras: Apostles, Our Lord, Mary I, Mary II, John the Evangelist, James the Lord's brother, Mark, 318 Orthodox, Athanasius, Basil, Gregory of Nyssa, Epiphanius, John Chrysostom, Cyril, Jacob of Serug, Gregory and Dioscorus; it adds that the book's index (p. 7) does not name the last explicitly as Dioscorus of Alexandria but calls it the anaphora with which the missal ends. The Enciclopedia Cattolica (vol. VII, 1951, 'Libri liturgici', third-party transcription) instead reports 18 anaphoras for the Rome 1945 book; the count stays unreconciled until the book is inspected. Compared with the inspected Asmara headings, the 17-anaphora list is consistent with the Keren study's three additions; equivalence of the Asmara Dionysius and Däbrä Zäyt headings with 1945 titles is unverified. Revision documents of 1940 and 1944 are recorded separately (geez-congregatio-orientalis-1940-1944-revision-documents).

source_record.note: Title and the declaration (Յայտարարութիւն) inspected. The declaration, dated at Pera, Constantinople, on 6 January 1879 and signed by Anton Petros IX, Patriarch of the House of Cilicia, recalls the long-sought uniformity of the Mass rite, the 1847 Constantinople national assembly held with Holy See permission, and a later decision of the patriarchate's bishops on a uniform Mass book. Bibliography entry 3385 gives 174 + 388 pages and one plate. The delivered scan holds the title, the declaration, the 388-page lection part (printed pp. 1-379 plus index) and a separately paginated 36-page Կանոնագրութիւն թիւ Պատարագի (low-Mass rubrics and chants, PDF 95-114) bound within the lections, but no 174-page sequence. Official retrospective identifies the text family as Lambron-Mec‘op‘. eastern-gaps batch 4 (2026-10-21): the declaration of 6 January 1879 (retained scan PDF 6–7) presents the book as an exemplar printed for the bishops' examination, with margins for observations, pending the next national synod and confirmation by the Apostolic See. Its fourth day of the Nativity (printed p. 12) reads 1 John 1:1–7 with John 21:20–25, not the 1 John 5:4–10 reported in Handēs 1906. eastern-gaps batch 5 (2026-10-22): the printed index (PDF 219) has separate Nativity and Epiphany sections; the fourth day of Epiphany (printed p. 19-20, PDF 15-16) reads 1 John 5:4-10 including the heavenly witnesses of verse 7. source_record.book_label: Ἀκολουθίαι τῶν ἀνωνύμων, 1738
source_record.church_scope: Roman attribution from BnF catalogue; individual Catholic community receipt unestablished
source_record.date: April 1738 printing; Roman imprint attributed by catalogue
source_record.note: The title includes the liturgies of Chrysostom, Basil and the Presanctified gifts; a bounded original Greek witness is acquired in full as offered. Rome and Propaganda Fide are catalogue attributions. Physical completeness, the catalogue 128+100 extent and a direct relationship to the 1754 Euchologion are unresolved. Finisher evidence (2026-10-19): the BnF record cb39303242b transcribes the same Greek title, including the office of Holy Communion, with April of AM 7246 / AD 1738, so identity and date are not disputed. In the offered 202-image witness the first pagination reaches printed p. 91 at provider PP97 (end of the Presanctified Liturgy), followed by an unnumbered dismissal leaf at PP98, whereas BnF gives [2]-128-100 pages; the Sunday Apostle and Gospel readings named on the title were not located in the bounded inspection, so the witness may lack about 36 pages of the first series. Raes (Enciclopedia Cattolica VII, 1951) reports a nine-volume Roman reprint of Arcudius's Anthologion in 1738, and BnF catalogues four further April 1738 Greek office books attributed to Propaganda; whether this volume belongs to such a set is unestablished. Cold review (2026-10-19): the dismissal leaf at PP98 ends with the catchword Ἀπος, which points to Apostle readings that the offered witness does not carry before the second pagination begins at PP99; this strengthens the inference that the Sunday Apostle and Gospel series named on the title is missing from this witness. Charon (Chrysostomika, 1908, printed p. 560) calls this book the Roman edition of the three Liturgies of 1738 and reports that its prototype was the Venice Euchologion of 1727, on which Benedict XIV's commission also based the 1754 Euchologion; that reported common source is recorded without adopting graph ancestry and does not establish direct dependence between 1738 and 1754.

source_record.church_scope: Ruthenian recension; Church mapping requires separate evidence
source_record.date_basis: Source and evidence type named in this row; publication, approval, effective date and retrospective attribution are not interchangeable.
source_record.note: MCI identifies Rome publication as a reform and the Slavonic basis of later English books. Referenced scan URL returns 404; no scan inspected. Additional public route on the UGCC commission page points to Google Drive file 0B4vzPDufLbhuYi1rLUJ6TWNPdms; whole-file request requires Google sign-in. No complete original-language scan acquired from this route. eastern-gaps batch 5 (2026-10-22): the Internet Archive item Sluzebnik1952 (588 images; SHA-256 39b014c7…) is the Rome 1952 photolithographic reissue; its colophon (printed p. 678) dates the original printing to June 1942 at the Grottaferrata monastery press, ordered by Pius XI and completed under Pius XII through the Congregation for the Eastern Church; 678 pages as Raes reports. Inspected pp. 231–232, 250–251, 677–678. No original 1942 title leaf seen; the 1944 imprimatur Kolupaev reports is not in this copy.
source_record.recension_identity_note: Raes 1947 pp. 85–87 explicitly distinguishes parallel Russian and Ruthenian series, both completed 1942. The 1940/1941 single-liturgy issues precede this complete book; physical format is not a substantive version boundary.
source_record.reception_evidence: The Slovenian translator identifies the 1942 Church Slavonic book as his source and reports the Križevci bishop’s confirmation request (3 June 2022, 92/2022) and dicastery approval (30 November 2022, 152/2022). This documents one approved translation source; original letters and general adoption remain unverified. Regional lane addition (byzantine_regional, 2026-10-19): the IKA report of 27 May 2023 independently names the Rome 1942 Church Slavonic Liturgikon of the Ruthenian recension as the source of the Slovenian translation, issued in three role editions (Služebnik for clergy, Božja liturgija for people and singers, and a notated edition) with episcopal approval no. 14/2023. Separately, the Croatian Chrysostom book printed in February 2018 names a different source, the Rome 1970 Ruthenian-recension Chrysostom printing (PDF/printed p. 4). Neither establishes use of the 1942 book in Croatia generally or in Serbia. Slavic-lane addition (byzantine_slavic, 2026-10-19): Kolupaev (2012, p. 390) examined the 1952 Rome 'Литургикон сиесть служебник' (679 pp.) and states it is a photolithographic reissue of the 1942 book; a Russian Catholic parish library lists the 1952 Liturgikon at 678 pp., Raes's page count for 1942. Slovak scholarship that names the 1952 Liturgikon as binding and as a translation source (Boháč; Mojzes) therefore points to the 1942 text. The UGCC commission's official-books page lists 'Служебник, Рим 1942' as the Church's Church Slavonic Sluzhebnyk. Keleher (p. 23 n. 33) also reports the 1952 Holy See reprint. Kolupaev (p. 388) notes a Tisserant imprimatur dated 17 May 1944 prefacing the 1942 Ruthenian text, a date later than the 1942 imprint; whether the copy he described was a later issue is unresolved. The commission's Google Drive copy of 1942 (file 0B4vzPDufLbhuYi1rLUJ6TWNPdms) still returns a Google sign-in page.

source_record.reception_note: Slipyj, 12 April 1942, reports use of the new Liturgikon at the Lviv seminary and objections among some Stanislaviv priests after initial submission. Slavic-lane addition (byzantine_slavic, 2026-10-19): Keleher (2006, pp. 20-21) reports a two-colour Lviv reprint of the new Chrysostom by Metropolitan Andrey in 1942 (5,000 copies, for clergy) and a black-and-white reprint by the Mukachevo eparchy in 1944, probably under Bishop Theodore Romzha. A 1962 Graz photolithographic Chrysostom of 151 pp. held by a Russian Catholic parish library in Saint Petersburg matches Raes's page count for the 1941 small Ruthenian issue; page-count identity is circumstantial. Kolupaev's 1978 small-format Chrysostom reissue repeats the Russian-use (Vulgata) 1941 issue he describes, which includes the troparion 'Господи иже Пресвятаго Твоего Духа' that the Ruthenian recension omits, so it is not a witness of this recension. The Košice eparchy calls the Roman books binding and dates the Ruthena Chrysostom 1941; Boháč names the 1940 Grottaferrata Chrysostom as the Slovak translation source.

source_record.note: Charon reports the Euchologion revision of Meletios Karmé at three dates that he does not reconcile: 1633 for the revision according to a Jerusalem manuscript (Holy Sepulchre ar. 127; printed p. 532); approval of the Vatican copy, Vat. ar. 618, by Patriarch Macarius III in 1643, with its dispatch to Pope Alexander VII for printing at Rome in 1662 (p. 532); and, in the Euchologion section, a recension 'made by Meletios Karmé in 1643' (p. 615), a 357-folio paper quarto. Nassif's 2018 title attaches 1635 to Karmé's Euchologion and calls the Roman project abortive. Charon (pp. 615-623) reports the failed Roman printing. source_record.note: Official Lungro sources identify the inter-eparchial Arbëresh Chrysostom Liturgy, Congregation approval and actual continued parish use. Lajme 2015 printed p. 49 explicitly names Liturgjia Hyjnore e atit tonë ndër shëjtrat Joan Hrysostomit (reported 1968, S. Nilo Grottaferrata) and says it remains used in Lungro Arbëresh parishes. The bishop’s 2018 pastoral PDF pp. 30–31 identifies Greek–Albanian and Albanian–Italian approved formats and says Albanian is commonly used in almost all its parishes. This meets received-service-book-language scope and is not blanket-deferred solely as a translation. A newly acquired Greek–Albanian Roma 1967 setting has an original title and a colophon dating completion of printing at S. Nilo, Grottaferrata, to 15 December 1967. Its generic Holy See approval leaf names no dated instrument/protocol. This establishes that exact setting, while identity with the retrospectively reported 1968 printing and other reported bilingual formats remains unresolved; a particular Lungro receiving copy and exact Greek exemplar are not authenticated. Lajme 2023 p. 104 gives decree publication 6 August 1968; the 2018 pastoral p. 30 says adoption decreed 13 October 1968. These reports do not authorize a silently harmonized exact adoption day. No Piana, Grottaferrata or Albanian Catholic local reception is inferred. Batch 4 (2026-10-21): OPAC SBN PAL0225860 catalogues a Greek–Albanian Liturgjia Hyjnore (catalogue title e atit tone shetrat Joan Hrysostomit) published in Rome in 1967 by the Associazione Cattolica Italiana per l'Oriente Cristiano, 182 p., 21 cm, with copies at Padua and Piana degli Albanesi. The extent is compatible with the inspected Roma 1967 setting, but catalogue identity is not proof of the same setting, and the Piana holding is not reception.

source_record.book_label: The Liturgical Prayer Books of the Melkite Greek Catholic Church, four volumes in six parts
source_record.church_scope: Melkite Catholic Church
source_record.date: decree of 1996; exclusive use from Pascha 1997; publication 1997–2000
source_record.date_basis: Date identifies only the event named in date_role; it is not composition, universal adoption or a period of use.
source_record.note: Volume I part 1 September–November and part 2 December–February (Horologion, Paraklitike, Menaion); volume II part 1 February–April and part 2 Holy Week (Triodion); volume III Paschaltide, April–June (Pentecostarion); volume IV June–August (Horologion, Paraklitike, Menaion). In large and small formats. One corpus of complementary parts, not six versions; it is the modern Catholic revision of the Triodion, Pentecostarion and Menaia. The letter states no year per part. The DLI record 44455 (Kitab as-salawat at-taqdisiyah, Jounieh, Paulist press, printed with the permission of Patriarch Maximos V, 'corrected translation on the basis of the Greek original') dates the parts: vol. III (22 March to end of June) 1997; vol. I.1 (1 September to end of November) and I.2 (1 December to end of February) 1998; vol. IV (18 May to end of August) 1999; vol. II.1 (15 January to 25 April) and II.2 (Great Holy Week) 2000. Its date ranges per part differ from the letter's month labels because of the movable cycles. The parts were not acquired.

source_record.book_label: Roman Greek liturgical book series, 1873-1902: all Byzantine liturgical books except the Typikon, in 16 volumes (reported by Raes)
source_record.church_scope: Greek-rite Catholics served by Roman Greek editions; reception unestablished
source_record.date_basis: Date identifies only the event named in date_role; it is not composition, universal adoption or a period of use.
source_record.note: Raes (Enciclopedia Cattolica VII, 1951; English rendering read whole) reports that from 1873 to 1902 all the Byzantine liturgical books except the Typikon were printed at Rome in 16 volumes, and that the Horologion edition was resumed in 1937. The lane labels five Roman books of 1873-1886 from the DLI catalogue (Euchologion 1873, Horologion 1876, Euangelion 1880, Apostolos 1881, Oktoechos 1886); their membership of the 16 is inferred from the date range only, and the other volumes (for example a Triodion, Pentecostarion, Paraklitike and Menaia, which carry Eucharistic propers) are unidentified. Raes's bibliography cites C. Korolevsky on the Roman edition of the Greek Menaia (Bollettino della Badia greca di Grottaferrata 3, 1949, and 4, 1950) as the next source. No chronology bounds are assigned to a range of printings.

source_record.book_label: Innovations in the Divine Liturgy introduced by Archbishop Angelo of Rossano (elected 1266), as attacked by Theodore of Cursi
source_record.church_scope: Historical Italo-Greek use of the archdiocese of Rossano; no modern Church reception asserted
source_record.date: after 1266 (second half of the thirteenth century); exact year unknown
source_record.date_basis: Date identifies only the event named in date_role; it is not composition, universal adoption or a period of use.
source_record.note: Parenti (section 3, notes 45-46, citing G. Mercati's study of Theodore of Cursi's Antirrhetikos) reports that the archbishop suppressed the three opening antiphons, the litany and prayer for the catechumens and the first series of petitions, simplified the opening invocation of the litanies and the Trisagion, and moved the preparation of the bread and wine to after the Gospel in imitation of the Roman offertory. These are named changes to order and prayers, known from a polemical witness reported in a secondary article; no service book carrying them is identified and their extent and duration are unknown. No chronology bounds are assigned.

source_record.book_label: Kritsfalusi György, Hungarian translation of the Liturgy of John Chrysostom (manuscript, 1795)
source_record.church_scope: Hungarian Greek Catholics (Mukachevo eparchy era)
source_record.date_basis: Date identifies the event stated in chronology_kind (manuscript-date), not composition, approval of another book or a period of use.
source_record.note: According to the latest, not yet refuted view reported by Dobos 2020 (printed p. 392), the first complete Hungarian translation of the Liturgy of Chrysostom, made by György Kritsfalusi and offered to Bishop András Bacsinszky as a name-day gift in 1795; it was kept in the Uzhhorod episcopal library and published by Sztripszky in 1913. Its closest affinity to the Moscow 1658 Služebnik is a scholarly inference. Open: original manuscript, present location and precise Slavonic exemplar unseen.
source_record.source_title_status: Description in the catalogue; no title inspected

sources.inspection: Reports the latest, not yet refuted view that Kritsfalusi's translation of 1795 is the first complete Hungarian translation; manuscript M–769 copied by István Lupess in 1814 is a variant of it, although a later owner attributed the translation to Mihály Krucsay in 1793; a copy made by Antal Papp at Hajdúdorog in 1854 is also mentioned. The 1882 title page names the book the translation of a nine-member committee of the Mukachevo and Prešov consistories (Hajdúdorog 1879); the book carries no ecclesiastical approval; 1890 added Basil, the Presanctified and priestly office texts. Note 39 records Bishop Dudás's 1954 instruction (ordinance 819 in circular 1954/XIII). Source-affinity arguments point to the Moscow edition of 1658, not to a located exemplar.

source_record.book_label: Calendar reform of the Hajdúdorog eparchy (Gregorian calendar from 24 June 1916)
source_record.church_scope: Hajdúdorog eparchy (with parallel decisions in Mukachevo and Prešov, later reversed or made optional there)
source_record.date_basis: Date identifies the event stated in chronology_kind (effective-date), not composition, approval of another book or a period of use.
source_record.language: Hungarian (circular); applies to the calendar of the liturgical books
source_record.note: Bishop Miklósy's circular 1990/1916 (Körlevelek VI (1916) 25) moved the feasts to the Gregorian calendar from 24 June 1916 after a meeting of 4 May 1916 with the Mukachevo and Prešov bishops, reporting that Pope Benedict XV's approval had been sought; supplementary circular 3150/1916 (Körlevelek XI (1916) 52) made separate provision for the Exaltation of the Cross, St Demetrius and the Protection of the Theotokos (Athanasiana 26, printed pp. 65–68, note 8). Mukachevo restored the Julian calendar on 21 November 1918 and Prešov made it optional; in 1919 some Hajdúdorog parishes had returned to it. Open: no continuous uniform implementation is claimed; the circular originals were not seen.

source_record.language: Hungarian, with the canonical parts (anaphoras) of the liturgies also printed in Greek
source_record.note: Revised against the Greek and expanded edition combining the 1882 and 1890 volumes, with the offices of the liturgical day, the Great Canon, dismissals, Sunday propers, calendar and a paschalion for 1921–1960. Its preface states that the canonical parts of the liturgies were printed in Greek as well, so that clergy could celebrate the essential part in the Church's original language until Greek liturgikons could be obtained from Rome (Athanasiana 27 (2008), printed p. 20, quoting the book's 'Emlékezetül', pp. 309–310). Distribution was announced by circular 1195 and the text made binding by circular 1021 of 1921. Open: do not date all public use from the private-use permission alone; book not acquired. Follow-up 2026-10-20: Ivancsó 2007, pp. 69–73, and Ivancsó 2008, pp. 19–25, re-inspected. The approval formula is permission for private use and must remain explicit. Dated circular 1021/1921 directs the revised book’s wording; circular 2351/1949 describes the heavily worn Chrysostom section of 1920 copies and orders a replacement extract. This documents operative local reception without establishing papal approval, public-use permission from 1920 alone, first celebration or universal compliance. The 1984 printing is reported as an unchanged reprint, not a new recension. Batch 3 follow-up (2026-10-20): all four offered photographs of seller item 32188629463 inspected. The unnumbered title leaf directly controls the reproduced 1920 title, private-use formula 1235/1920, revised/expanded statement and Jóba Elek printer line 1723–1920, but original-impression authentication is unresolved because the 1984 facsimile retains that imprint. Whole contents, dated approval verso and Emlékezetül remain unacquired. College record bibNY56K501 supplies exact separate copies Ant10911/M-1638, Ant10792/M-1637 (missing pp. 273–311, with catalogued August 1920 preparatory annotations), and Ant101011/M-1891 (Hajdúböszörmény parish stamps); annotations and stamps were not seen. No first-use or public-altar-use claim follows.
source_record.source_title_status: 1920-imprint title directly inspected in seller photograph; physical impression not independently authenticated
source_record.substantive_feature: Greek text of the canonical parts beside Hungarian; Basil and Presanctified joined to Chrysostom; offices of the day, calendar and paschalion 1921–1960 (Athanasiana 27 (2008), printed pp. 20–21)
source_record.witness_limit: Four offered seller photographs acquired and inspected: front cover, spine/cover, endpapers, and an unnumbered title leaf. Only the fourth photograph carries printed book text. It verifies the reproduced title, 1235/1920 private-use permission, revised/expanded editorial statement and Jóba Elek printer line 1723–1920. No permission-date verso, contents, Greek anaphora pages, terminal leaves or Emlékezetül pp. 309–310 are shown. The seller calls the book a 1920 first edition, but the physical impression cannot be independently authenticated from these four photographs: the known 1984 facsimile retains the 1920 imprint. No full 1920 book or complete textual state is acquired. A binding appearance cannot establish a print date. Full catalogue records read, original physical copies and annotations not inspected. The catalogue lists three separate copies, including an incomplete annotated copy; they must not be merged with the seller copy. No digital object or MARC 856 field is present in the returned record. Parish stamps and ownership annotations do not by themselves date liturgical use. Catalogue transcription is an acquisition route, not a replacement for original-book collation.

Open: book not acquired; the title-page permission number differs between Ivancsó 2003 and 2008; Dokumentáció I (2006), pp. 53–54, not seen. Follow-up 2026-10-20: Ivancsó 2007, pp. 69–73, and Ivancsó 2008, pp. 19–25, re-inspected. The approval formula is permission for private use and must remain explicit. Dated circular 1021/1921 directs the revised book’s wording; circular 2351/1949 describes the heavily worn Chrysostom section of 1920 copies and orders a replacement extract. This documents operative local reception without establishing papal approval, public-use permission from 1920 alone, first celebration or universal compliance. The 1984 printing is reported as an unchanged reprint, not a new recension. Batch 3 follow-up (2026-10-20): the college catalogue bibNY56K11755 / recnum 10613 identifies four copies (D 442, DT 399, DT 484 and C 12647) and independently catalogues the permission as 1650/1949. This is catalogue corroboration of Ivancsó 2003, not original-title verification or adjudication of the 2008 discrepancy. DT 484 contains typed pp. 60–80 and C 12647 five typed prayer pages; neither supplement creates a new printed edition or full recension. No full original 1949 book acquired.

source_record.church_scope: Roman Ruthenian-recension printing; cited as the source of the Croatian Križevci translation of 2018; general reception not established
source_record.date_basis: Date identifies the event stated in chronology_kind (source-publication-as-cited), not composition, approval of another book or a period of use.
source_record.note: The exact source imprint is stated on PDF/printed p. 4 of the Croatian 2018 book. It belongs to the Roman Ruthenian line already held as byz-ruthenian-chrysostom-1940 (Chrysostom issue) and byz-ruthenian-1942 (Liturgikon, same Grottaferrata press); whether it is a later printing of the 1940 issue or differs substantively has not been established, so no new textual state is asserted. Open: coordinate identity with the byzantine_slavic lane before admission; the original 1970 copy was not acquired. Slavic-lane addition (byzantine_slavic, 2026-10-19): No source examined by this lane names a 1970 Ruthenian Chrysostom printing: the UGCC commission's official list gives only the 1942 Church Slavonic Sluzhebnik, Keleher names the 1941 issue and its 1942 Lviv and 1944 Mukachevo reprints, and Kolupaev's survey of Grottaferrata Slavonic books (from copies available to him) omits it. Kolupaev records that 1941 books he presents as printings for Russian-tradition faithful were later repeated: the Presanctified in a 1962 photomechanical reprint made at Graz, Austria, the Vespers in 1968, the Basil in 1969 and the small-format Chrysostom in 1978, with a second 1978 Chrysostom repeating the 1949 edition (2012, pp. 390-391). He also identifies the 1952 Liturgikon as a photolithographic reissue of the 1942 book (p. 390) and records a 1970 photolithographic second edition of an Orthodox St James Liturgy at the same press (p. 392). By analogy with this reissue practice, the 1970 Ruthenian-recension Chrysostom is probably a later printing of the Roman Ruthenian Chrysostom text held as byz-ruthenian-chrysostom-1940 rather than a new textual state. This is an inference, not an inspected finding, and the 1970 printing remains a separate printing witness, not a duplicate. Inspection of its title verso or colophon for a reprint statement remains the deciding check.
source_record.source_title_status: Transliterated title as cited in the Croatian 2018 book; original title leaf not inspected

N. 64/2016), and gives the imprint: Ordinarijat Križevačke eparhije, printed by Crobook, 1000 copies, ISBN 978-953-59968-0-4, printed February 2018. source_record.church_scope: Kyivan Uniate metropolia; first Sluzhebnik printed specifically for Catholic Ruthenians (Huculak); later Church mapping requires reception evidence
source_record.date: 1617 (title, Cyrillic numerals); dedication to Lev Sapieha dated Vilnius 1 January 1617 (Kniga Belarusi)
source_record.date_basis: Date identifies the event stated in chronology_kind (publication, approval or attestation as named), not composition or a period of use.
source_record.note: Title leaf inspected: three liturgies and the Presanctified, issued at the expense of Chancellor Lev Sapieha at the Mamonych press. Kniga Belarusi no. 80 gives the collation (29 + 26 unnumbered leaves, pp. 1-473) and contents: Nauka for priests, Proskomedia order, Chrysostom, Basil, Presanctified, blessing of wine, Vespers and Matins orders, dismissals and prayers. Huculak (App. II) calls it the first Sluzhebnik produced for Catholic Ruthenians, without ecclesiastical approval, its Nauka mixing Eastern and Latin practice, and distinguishes it from the Orthodox Holy Spirit Brotherhood Sluzhebnik of the same year (Kniga Belarusi no. 81).
source_record.reception_evidence: Huculak (App. II, p. 386) reports that Bishop Vojna-Orans'kyj of Pinsk (1647-1653), answering Sakowicz's charge that Catholic Ruthenians used Orthodox texts, replied that Catholics were using this Mamonych edition (citing Wawryk). A secondary report of mid-17th-century use in the Pinsk eparchy, not a date of adoption.

source_record.version_boundary_basis: Catalogue and repertoire contents: a Nauka (instruction) for priests absent from the Brotherhood edition of 1617 (Huculak, App. II; Kniga Belarusi nos. 80-81).

source_record.date_basis: Date identifies the event stated in chronology_kind (publication, approval or attestation as named), not composition or a period of use.
source_record.note: Kolupaev pp. 390-391: contents Vespers, Compline, Midnight Office, Matins, Liturgy, various orders, menologion, prokeimena and appendices; differs from contemporary Moscow Patriarchate Sluzhebniks by lacking the Izvestie uchitelnoe and naming the feast of All Saints of the Russian land 'в земле русстей'. The parish library catalogue identifies the 1983 book explicitly as Recensione Volgata. Cold review (2026-10-19): the differences Kolupaev lists are against Moscow Patriarchate Sluzhebniks, not against the Roman 1942 or 1953 books. He cites the feast title 'в земле русстей' at p. 47 of the 1983 book (2012, p. 391). Semenenko-Basin and Caprio place the same feast, in the same wording, in the menologion appendix of the 1953 issue at second pagination pp. 47-48 (2021, pp. 382-383). The 1953 issue is the 1942 Vulgata book reissued with appendices, so the 1983 book is probably a reprint of the 1953 issue. Kolupaev's reference list is missing from the delivered PDF, so his reference [12] was not resolved.

source_record.note: Mosul Dominican press, 96 printed pages; complementary 1901 Proprium and 1900 lection books remain distinct volumes. Printed p 35/PDF 67 includes the life-giving Gospel phrase absent in 1767 printed p 284/PDF 339; both native readings independently checked. This bounded difference is not an exhaustive revision inventory or a complete annual Eucharistic book set. Chaldean lane addition (2026-10-19): Coakley and Taylor (no. 58) give [ii], 406 pp.: ordinary pp. 1–96 and proper pp. 97–406, sold with or without the proprium, the ordinary also issued separately; the Bonn Proprium (record chald-proper-1901) is therefore the second part of the same Missale. Coakley reports a Syriac imprimatur of Patriarch Joseph Emmanuel II dated 15 August 1900 and, citing Delly (OCP 23 (1957) 170), issue only in April 1902 despite the 1901 title date. Reprints: Mosul 1936 (reset, with minor variants recorded by Macomber), Paris 1982 and Atour Publications about 2005. The three 1900 lection volumes are now acquired (record chaldean-mosul1900-lections). eastern-gaps batch 5 (2026-10-22): Delly (OCP 23, 1957, pp. 162-170, read on images) documents from Propaganda letters that Propaganda paid for the Dominican printing while granting no direct or indirect approval, that the text was disputed among the bishops after Patriarch Khayyat's death (6 November 1899), and that publication was announced on 21 March 1902.

Mando 2012, Chaldean patriarchal press list, item 3
source_record.note: Reported reprint of the 1901 ordinary (Coakley citing Delly 1957, p. 170; Sako 2025), printed at the Chaldean patriarchal press in Mosul rather than the Dominican press (Mando; Sako). Macomber cites both Mosul editions at pp. 24–36, but his apparatus records the 1936 printing apart from 1901 at anaphora line 2 (p. 358, a singular reading shared with the oldest witnesses) and line 52 (p. 366, a variant word form). It is a reset printing with at least minor variants, not a facsimile; the extent and nature of those changes are uncollated. eastern-gaps batch 5 (2026-10-22): Delly (OCP 23, 1957, p. 170, read on image) states that the 1901 (in reality 1902) missal was reprinted in 1936 at the patriarchal press in Mosul and was in use in all Chaldean dioceses, Persia included, by 1957.

source_record.book_label: Liturgia sanctorum Apostolorum Adaei et Maris ... necnon ordo baptismi (Urmia 1890)
source_record.church_scope: Assyrian Church of the East; Archbishop of Canterbury's mission imprint
source_record.date_basis: Date identifies the event stated in chronology_kind, not composition, adoption or a period of use.
source_record.note: Macomber's Ur. Collateral; not Catholic. The inserted English list of mission books (PDF 175) says the words of institution were printed as in 1 Corinthians 11 although found only in very modern Mosul manuscripts, and Macomber records Ur inserting the institution narrative (p. 365 n. 1): an editorial insertion, not a manuscript reading. Sako's 1890 Urmia printing attributed to the Lazarist Paul Bedjan is not shown to be this book. eastern-gaps batch 4 (2026-10-21): the title photograph Sako published with his 27 August 2025 article (captioned Urmia 1890) matches this scan's Syriac title setting at PDF 174 line for line, including the red title lines and the Syriac imprint lines; the book Sako illustrates is therefore this Anglican mission edition, whose Latin imprint names the Archbishop of Canterbury's mission press. His attribution of the 1890 printing to Bedjan is not supported by the imprint; the photographed copy bears a Baghdad Chaldean institutional stamp naming Simon Peter (Shimʿun al-Safa), which shows holding, not liturgical use. eastern-gaps batch 5 (2026-10-22): Delly (OCP 23, 1957, pp. 161 n. 5 and 165, read on images) records Thomas Audo's 9 July 1895 critique of the missal printed at Urmia by the Anglicans and states that the Anglicans published a missal for the Nestorians in 1890; Vosté (OCP 11, 1945, p. 73) reports Propaganda's 24 March 1890 withdrawal of the Chaldean missal project from Paul Bedjan, who thereafter no longer dealt with liturgical books. Sako's attribution of a 1890 Urmia printing of the three Masses to Bedjan is therefore contradicted by Vosté's archival account and unsupported by Delly, who names only the Anglican missal; this Anglican edition remains the only identified 1890 Urmia printing, though neither study lists every Urmia imprint (cold review 2026-10-22).

source_record.note: eastern-gaps batch 5 (2026-10-22): Archbishop Thomas Audo of Urmia's missal; 11, 245 pp. The approbation leaf attests concordance with the Rome 1767 missal after collation (Audo) and carries the nihil obstat of Franciscus Lesné, Apostolic Delegate in Persia; the French preface says it places the Sunday and feast Epistles and Gospels and the proper chants (introit, pre-Epistle verse, gradual, offertory, communion) in the missal, keeps the 1767 ordinary followed at Urmia and Salmas rather than the unfixed Mesopotamian practice, and disclaims imposing a new missal on the Chaldean Church. source_record.language: Arabic (other languages of the printed book not established)
source_record.limitations: The 'before' column of the comparison is quoted from an Orthodox Euchologion, so the exact Catholic pre-1990 wording is not established. The provisional text and its relation to the 1980 and 1987 printings are unknown.
source_record.note: A proposal of 27 April 1975 by Bishop Youhanna Nouier of Asyut and a synodal commission of 18 May 1976 led to a provisional text issued for comment and then to a final text issued on 25 February 1990 under Patriarch Stephanos II. The before/after table shows a reworded preparation prayer, a thanksgiving prayer reduced from three sections with responses to one paragraph, a shortened anaphora opening and a reworded epiclesis; ritual actions are said to be unchanged.

The catalogue transcribes a memorial note in Ant30125: in 1856 Sándor Nehrebeczky brought this Sluzhebnik from Lemberg at his own cost and offered it for the use of the Sátoraljaújhely Greek Catholic church, whose ex libris is on the title page; the same note records his death in 1881, so it was written retrospectively after that date. Like the route's other received-copy witnesses (Timár, Abod, Eger), the record is held for origin review, not as a route candidate. The edition itself is the separate record byzantine-slavic-przemysl1840; this record adds no textual version.

source_record.church_scope: Syro-Malabar Catholic Church
source_record.date_basis: Year is the identified publication or reported release, not composition or universal adoption
source_record.note: Book-stated date 1845 preserved. The 1904 permission (1906 book, PDF 508) authorizes printing after the exemplar 'ejusdem Missalis' printed by Propaganda in 1775 and again in 1845, and says that in that exemplar the Ordo Missae is dispersed and the Rogation lessons stand in a supplement. Tisserant (DTC XIV.2, col. 3158) records a Propaganda reprint of 1844, Ordo chaldaicus rituum et lectionum, with the 60-page Ordo Missae usually bound after p. 440, which matches that description. The sacramental ritual, Ordo Chaldaicus Ministerii Sacramentorum, was also printed by Propaganda in 1775 and 1845 (Pallath 2023 p. 41; the 1845 edition verified from the 1946 Alwaye reprint, CMS India excerpt); it shares the years only and is not this exemplar. Whether the permission's 1845 denotes the 1844 Missal reprint or a separate issue remains unresolved until a title page is seen. Do not count a separate substantive version.

source_record.church_scope: Syro-Malabar
source_record.date_basis: Imprimatur date printed on PDF 8; entry into force on the same day reported by Pallath 2023 p. 26. The 20 January 1962 instruction concerns the Syriac missal, not this book.
source_record.language: Malayalam (institution narrative and g'hanta prayers kept in Syriac) followed by a complete Syriac section
source_record.note: Commission reports Malayalam publication. Pallath 2023 (pp. 25-26, n. 47) and the 1985 decree printed in the 1986 book distinguish two events: the instruction of 20 January 1962 that promulgated the restored Syriac missal printed at Alwaye (the 1960 Taksa, malabar-1960-taksa), and the entry into force on 3 July 1962, by decision of the bishops, of this partly Malayalam book. Complete GPURA scan (142 PDF pages) acquired in research scratch: title leaf (PDF 7) 'സീറോമലബാർ സഭയുടെ കുർബാനക്രമം', Mar Thoma Sleeha Press, Alwaye 1962; imprimatur of seven bishops dated 3 July 1962 (PDF 8); Malayalam order to printed p. 58, then a separately paginated Syriac section bound from the back (sampled PDF 100 and 135). Pallath describes that section as the complete restored Syriac text reproduced; it witnesses that text and is not a new Syriac version unless collation shows change. The approved operative Malayalam order is received Syro-Malabar service-book language under guidance/time-machine.md §11. Batch 5: the Syriac part (PDF 75-138) is the 1960 Alwaye Taksa with its own title leaf, 12 May 1960 concordat and imprimatur and printed pp. 1-62; Malayalam order ends at printed 58 (PDF 72), PDF 73-74 blank. The instruction of 20 January 1962 is now read in Pallath 2019 (pp. 206-209, Latin pp. 387-389).
source_record.scope_note: The approved operative Malayalam order is received Syro-Malabar service-book language under guidance/time-machine.md §11. The separately paginated Syriac section witnesses the restored Syriac text; its distinctness from the 1960 Taksa is uncollated. The 20 January 1962 instruction promulgated the Syriac missal, while the Malayalam book entered into force on 3 July 1962 by the bishops' decision.

source_record.date_basis: No chronology: the Eucharistic layer has no stated date, and the 1529 colophon belongs to another layer.
source_record.note: Assemani (codex LXVI, 128 folios) dates the body to 1529 by its epigraph at f. 94 ff., a pontifical copied at the monastery of Mar Acha near Gazarta from an exemplar of 1276, but excepts the first ten and last twenty-eight leaves, which 'appear' (videntur) to have been added by Joseph, bishop of the Indies, scribe of codices XLVI, LXII and LXV. The anaphoras (Apostles; Theodore at f. 116v) fall within those added leaves. The 1545 date in secondary catalogues is an ownership note at f. 98v. syri.ac also lists a form of consecration of bread and wine rendered from Latin into Syriac (folio not located). source_record.church_scope: Syro-Malankara Catholic Church

source_record.language: Syriac; exact language distribution and native title uninspected
source_record.note: Contemporary account specifies Xystus and short James anaphoras. The 1886 and 1931 Pampakuda books have different selections. No direct descent from the 1922 Sharfeh asserted. Syriac-Malankara lane addition (2026-10-19): Lugmayr (2013, pp. 242-243, after Madey 1973) reports that Mar Ivanios had only Xystus and James reprinted at the Jacobite Pampakuda press and that the institution narrative of the first was assimilated to the direct form of the second; the Enciclopedia Cattolica (English web rendering) adds prayers including an absolution formula. Both are secondary reports. Batch 5 context (Pallath 2023 documents): a letter quoted in Rahmani's report of 12 May 1927 (dated 1925 and linked to the Ivanios party by the editor) offered to accept the Syriac Catholic printed Missal and Ritual; by 17 March 1928 Ivanios held the Syriac Catholic patriarchate's printed missal and found it the same as his own except for the pope's commemoration and the filioque; on 4-5 July 1930 the Holy See kept the liturgical books described as coming from Propaganda, subject to examination by Bishops Kalacherry and Benziger; in September 1930 the reunited bishops said Mass according to the Catholic missal of the Syrian rite of Antioch. None of this identifies the 1934 book's text.

source_record.note: Repertoire reduction is reported, but the exact count is unresolved: the official introduction says eight, while the reviewed Maronite stage dossier records nine in Dib/Beggiani. Original title, colophon and removed titles remain uninspected; do not invent a reconciliation. Maronite lane addition (2026-10-19): the ONB copy's title page reads Rome 1762 (Komarek's Typographia Linguarum Orientalium), and its approbation by J. S. Assemani, Vatican Library, is dated 10 April 1763 and states that the missal was collated with the missal printed by Propaganda Fide in 1716 and found to agree with it. Both dates therefore stand on one book: title 1762, approbation 1763. The approbation's statement of agreement fits the 1992 introduction's description of later editions as copies of 1716 apart from trimming; it does not by itself settle the anaphora count, which remains unverified. Canvas 4 of the same copy, the last text page in reading order (catchword REIM.), carries a Garshuni printer's note that names Rome and appears to give a month and year of completion; it has not been transcribed, and its date must be read before the 1762 title and 1763 approbation are treated as the book's complete date evidence. eastern-gaps batch 4 (2026-10-21): anaphora headings read on the Austrian National Library copy, canvases 226, 196, 183, 156, 137, 116, 103 and 094: Peter head of the Apostles, Twelve Apostles, Xystus, John, Mark, Eustathius, Roman Church and John Maron, each with its own institution narrative; then a Good Friday order headed anaphora of the signing of the holy chalice (canvas 072). Whether Dib's and Beggiani's 'nine' counts that order is not stated by them. The printer's note on canvas 4 is only partly read. eastern-gaps batch 5 (2026-10-22): canvas 4 note re-read: completion of printing in Rome on 2 Nisan under Clement XIII (year tentative); Gemayel 1970 pp. 52-56 renders it as 2 April 1763 and describes an Antonine-funded reprint of 1716 omitting five anaphoras, naming Eustathius among them, while the ONB copy has Eustathius (canvas 116) and lacks James. Conflict unresolved.

A witness to manuscript copying after printing; its differences from 1594 are not examined.

source_record.note: The Malayalam preface (PDF 3 to 10, printed 1 to 8) says the book contains only the taksas of Mar Yakob and Mar Dionysius bar Salibi. It names Fr. P. T. Geevarghese, M.A. (later Mar Ivanios), among the priests who shared in the translation and revision. By order of Mar Dionysius, Metropolitan of the Malankara diocese, the Syriac scholar Malpan Mattackal Alexandros Kathanar examined the whole translation. This is a pre-reunion vernacular translation of a non-Catholic Church, so its history is deferred. It matters here only as a possible predecessor of the Syro-Malankara Malayalam Taksa line; a later secondary account says Mar Ivanios translated the Taksa into Malayalam in 1919. No Catholic use or textual descent is asserted.

source_record.note: Ziadé's first complete diaconicon, edited by Patriarch Ignatius Ephrem II Rahmani. The Arabic preface reports the deacon's text corrected against old manuscripts, Arabic limited to the Creed, Trisagion, diptychs, litanies and Lord's Prayer, a new part with Sunday and feast chants, and appended Arabic fraction hymns, and orders the book followed. The Bonn record's 1912 is contradicted by the printed title and spine (1905). A pencil note on the title page names a first edition (Beirut, Jesuit press, 1884, 44 pages) under the Syriac title Brightman gives for a Beirut 1888 minister's book; the preface itself says the book needed reprinting.

source_record.authority: The General Chapter of 1677, under Innocent Le Masson, Prior of the Grande Chartreuse and General of the Order
source_record.citation:
Printed on the engraved title page of the 1679 edition, READ HERE IN THE PAGE
IMAGE on 2026-08-02 and no longer taken from the catalogue: `MISSALE CARTVSIANI
/ Ordinis ex ordinatione Capituli Generalis. / Anno Domini M.D.C.LXXVII. /
Celebrati Sub R.P.D. Innocentio le Masson Priore / Cartusiæ ac totius eiusdem
ordinis Generali` [verified, canvas f5 of ark:/12148/bpt6k9127828m].

THE CATALOGUE'S TYPO IS THE CATALOGUE'S. Gallica's record transcribes the last
words as `totius eiusdem odinis generali`; the engraved plate reads `ordinis`
plainly. The earlier state of this row reproduced `odinis` and flagged it as the
catalogue's own -- that flag was right, and it is now settled at the plate
instead of being a guess about a transcription.

THE ORDINANCE ITSELF IS PRINTED IN THE BOOK, which is better evidence than the
title page and was not previously known to this file. Innocent Le Masson's
prefatory letter at canvas f7, headed `FRATER INNOCENTIVS, Humilis Prior Majoris
Cartusiæ, ac totius Ordinis Cartusiensis Minister Generalis`, recites it and
then quotes its tenor [verified in the page image]: `... ordinationem in Capitulo
Generali anni 1677. edidimus, cujus tenorem hic referre placet. [Quia Missalium
penuria laboramus, ordinamus Missalia ad vsum Ordinis de novo imprimi, ac
propterea monemus Visitatores Provinciarum & Priores Domorum, vt si quid in
ipsis ... addendum` -- the sentence runs onto the following leaf, which was not
fetched, and is therefore cut here at the catchword rather than completed from
guesswork.
source_record.date_note:
TWO YEARS ARE IN PLAY AND THEY ARE NOT COLLAPSED. The chapter met in 1677; the
book was printed in 1679. The station is dated by the PRINTING, 1679, because
that is the state the line reached, and the chapter's year is in `authority` and
in the citation rather than being averaged into the date.

BOTH YEARS ARE NOW VERIFIED ON ONE LEAF, which is the cleanest possible warrant
for keeping them apart: the engraved title plate at canvas f5 carries `Anno
Domini M.D.C.LXXVII.` in its title and `1679` in its imprint at the foot of the
same plate [verified 2026-08-02]. Le Masson's letter at f7 names the chapter
year a third time, as `Capitulo Generali anni 1677`.

source_record.citation: Sacred Congregation for Divine Worship, De editione typica altera, Prot. N. 1970/74, 27 March 1975, printed in the front matter of the 2002 typical edition; registered as work.holy-see.de-editione-typica-altera-missalis-romani-1975.
source_record.dateline: Ex aedibus Sacrae Congregationis pro Cultu Divino, die 27 martii Anni Sancti 1975, feria V in Cena Domini.
source_record.effect: No departure in this slice, and the act itself says why not.
source_record.effect_note:
THE ACT LISTS ITS OWN CHANGES AND NONE OF THEM IS IN THIS SLICE, which is a
better reason for an empty station than any this history has had before. Read
here: the description of the offices of acolyte and lector replaces those
treating of the subdeacon at nn. 142-152 of the Institutio generalis; certain
formularies of the ritual and votive Masses are completed with entrance and
communion antiphons; the Masses of the dedication of a church and altar, for
reconciliation, of the Blessed Virgin Mary Mother of the Church and of the Most
Holy Name of Mary are added; and further minor variations are made in titles and
rubrics. This slice carries the Ordinary and Holy Week, and the act touches
neither.

The acquisition audit calls this edition the postconciliar row with no whole
witness located anywhere -- what exists is the Ordo Missae alone, three orders of
magnitude too small. So the emptiness here is partly a real reading of the
decree and partly a bound on the corpus, and both are stated rather than one
being allowed to stand for the other.

act reaches past it to the edition, and that is recorded here rather than

source_record.citation:
Sacred Congregation of Rites, 9 December 1924, operative clause `Vaticana hujus
Missalis editio pro typica habenda est`, with later printings `omnino
conformandae erunt, ita ut in iis nihil immutare fas sit`; dateline `Die 9
Decembris 1924`, subscribed `A. Card. VICO, Ep. Portuen. et S. Rufinae, S. R. C.
Praefectus` and `Alexander Verde, S. R. C. Secretarius` [recorded, as above].
source_record.effect: No departure. No unit of this use has been read.
source_record.effect_note:
THIS STATION IS THE COUNTER-EXAMPLE THAT KEEPS A GENERALISATION HONEST, and it
is why the exempt-uses line is drawn the way it is. The two signatories here --
Cardinal Vico as Prefect and Alexander Verde as Secretary -- are THE SAME TWO MEN
who signed the Roman typical edition's decree of 25 July 1920, in the same
offices, four years apart. So the diocesan uses do not legislate their own
typical editions: Rome does, through the same congregation.

And yet no edge is drawn from the Roman line into this one. One congregation
acting for two rites is a fact about who signs, not a descent of one rite from
the other, and drawing it would make the Braga use look like a branch of the
Roman typical editions. The distinction between an authority and a lineage is
exactly what this file's edges exist to keep.

source_record.via_unrepresented_basis:
The same decree says the text was drawn from the other typical edition, that of
1900: `In qua editione, ex altera typica anni 1900 deprompta, illud tantum
innovatum est, quod ex recentibus praescriptionibus liturgicis et ex additionibus
et variationibus, in Breviario typico inductis, consequeretur.` That edition is
not in this corpus and no act promulgating it is cited here, so the edge from the
1634 revision down to 1920 crosses at least one station this record does not
hold. It is drawn as descent, not as succession.

The quotation also bounds the 1920 edition's own reach, and is why this act
carries so few departures: it says that the only thing made new was what followed
from the recent liturgical prescriptions and from the additions and variations
introduced in the typical Breviary.

source_record.act_citation_note:
CORRECTED 2026-08-01. This station carried `act_citation = "not-found"` from the
day it was drawn until the missal acquisition audit read the decree. The
correction, and why the error was made, are both worth keeping.

THE DECREE EXISTS AND HAS NOW BEEN READ, at page 2 of the Vatican typical
edition, in the exact facsimile this repository already had registered. Opening,
with the OCR damage of that text layer reproduced (`rubricanim`, `i960`):

  DECRETUM
  Novo rubricanim corpore, a Summo Pontifice Ioanne XXIII, Motu proprio
  << Rubricarum instructum >> diei 23 iulii anno i960 approbato posteroque die
  a Sacra Rituum Congregatione promulgato, vix fieri non potuit quin eadem
  Sacra Rituum Congregatio novam Missalis romani editionem, ad dictum
  rubricarum codicem plane accommodatam, pararet.

Operative clause: `hinc est quod praesens Vaticana Missalis romani editio uti
<< typica >> declaratur`. Dateline: `Romae, ex aedibus Sacrae Rituum
Congregationis, die 23 iunii 1962`, subscribed `A. M. Card. LARRAONA, S. R. C.
Praefectus` and `Henricus Dante, S. R. C. a secretis`.

So the incipit `Novo rubricarum corpore`, which this file expressly declined to
promote because it was known only from a report, is now read from the book.

WHY THE ERROR WAS MADE, because it is instructive and not careless. This
tracer's corpus is seven Internet Archive OCR text layers, and its 1962 witness
is the BENZIGER printing, which carries a New York imprimatur and not the
Vatican decree. The statement `only three occurrences of DECRETUM in 136,068

source_record.root_basis:
The record of this line starts here. The Braga use is far older -- a 1558
printing is at the Bibliotheque nationale de France and a 1498 printing is
recorded with no digital facsimile located -- and neither is carried in this run,
so no edge is drawn into this station.

That makes this line unusual and worth noticing: it is the ONLY use line in this
file whose root is an act rather than a printing.

THE 1558 PRINTING WAS REACHED AND READ ON 2026-08-02, and this root is kept
anyway. It is BnF Réserve B-1478, 554 canvases, `Missale juxta usum & ordinem
Almae Bracarensis Ecclesiae Hispaniarum Primatis`, dated 1558 by Gallica's own
record, and its shelfmark is pencilled on the flyleaf at canvas f4 beside the
reference `Weale 198` [verified]. Two things in it are worth a later lane's
attention and NEITHER IS ASSERTED AS AN ACT HERE:

  1.  IT CARRIES WHAT LOOKS LIKE ITS OWN PROMULGATING INSTRUMENT. Canvas f5 is a
      letter headed `BALTHASAR LIMPVS ARCHIEPISCOPVS ET BRACARAE Dominus,
      Hispaniarum Primas: Decano & Capitulo sanctae Bracarensis Ecclesiae, ac
      totius eius prouinciae Clero sanctum exoptat spiritum & salutem in Domino
      sempiternam`, in which Archbishop Baltasar Limpo describes finding the old
      missal `corruptum illud certe vetustate` and having a corrected edition
      made [verified in the page image]. That is an archbishop of Braga ordering
      a Braga missal, four hundred years before the act this line is rooted on.
      IT IS NOT ADDED AS A STATION IN THIS RUN: the letter was read but not
      transcribed whole, it carries no date in the portion read, and adding a
      root below an existing root is a change to the line's shape rather than an
      evidence upgrade. It is the single most promising lead for extending this
      line backwards and it is written down so it is not re-found.

  2.  IT WAS PRINTED AT LYON, NOT AT BRAGA. Gallica's record gives the imprint
      as `Lugduni sumptibus Jo. à Burgundia, bibliopolae regis Lusitanorum,
      1558` [verified] -- at Lyon, at the charge of Jean de Bourgogne, bookseller
      to the King of Portugal. Worth recording because this file carries a
      Lyonnais line as well, and a reader meeting `Lugduni` on a Braga book
      should not take it for a use.

  3.  ONE CAUTION ON THE COPY. Its first printed leaf in the digitisation is the
      Limpo letter; no printed title page was found in the leaves examined, and
      the BnF describes the preliminaries as `[10]` leaves. Whether the title
      leaf is absent from this copy was NOT established, and it is flagged
      rather than resolved.

source_record.act_citation_note:
THE INSTRUMENT WAS NOT READ HERE AND IS BELIEVED TO EXIST. Its title and date
come from two documents that were read at the bytes: Summorum Pontificum names
it `Quattuor Abhinc Annos` beside Ecclesia Dei, and this repository's passage
record for Ecclesia Dei states that the motu proprio's footnote `identifies the
letter Quattuor abhinc annos of 3 October 1984` [recorded:
src/sources/works/john-paul-ii/ecclesia-dei/editions/english-vatican-web-2026-07-25/passages/complete-text.toml].

So the act is named, dated and twice attested by later instruments, and its own
text has not been read. `not-found` is exactly that state, and it is not
`none-claimed`: an instrument is claimed here and is missing, which is a
different thing from a printing for which no instrument is claimed at all.
source_record.act_citation_scope:
ADDED 2026-08-01, and THE SEARCH IT RECORDS FOUND SOMETHING. This is section
7.2's correction happening a second time, caught this time by the rule that
correction produced.

Searched: THIS REPOSITORY'S OWN SOURCE LIBRARY, for `quattuor abhinc annos`,
case-insensitively. Four files answer. Two are inventories, one is the Ecclesia
Dei passage record this note already cites -- and the fourth is
src/sources/works/holy-see/acta-apostolicae-sedis/editions/volume-76-1984/edition.toml,
whose own notes read that the complete 1984 volume `carries the Congregation for
Divine Worship's letter of 3 October 1984 on the use of the Roman Missal of 1962
(Quattuor abhinc annos) at pp. 1088-1089`. That edition has a registered OCR PDF
artifact beneath it.

SO THE INSTRUMENT IS AT NAMED PAGES OF A VOLUME THIS REPOSITORY ALREADY HOLDS,
and `not-found` here means not in the missal corpus this slice reads. The value
is left as it stands because promoting it is a claim that somebody READ the
letter, and nobody has; naming a document and reading it are different acts. The
next lane to touch this station should open pages 1088-1089 of that artifact,
and the station should then become `cited-in-corpus`.

source_record.root_basis_superseded:
Superseded on 2026-08-01 by the edge above. What it said:

  The earliest act this tracer represents. It is not the beginning of the Roman
  Mass and is not offered as one: what stands before it -- the pre-Tridentine
  curial missal, the 1474 Milan printing, the diocesan uses out of which the
  Tridentine commission worked -- is a live question this tracer takes no
  position on and draws no edge into. A root here means "this record starts
  here", not "nothing preceded it".

Its parenthetical list is still right about the 1474 printing and the diocesan
uses: this slice draws NO edge from any of them into Quo primum either, and the
pre-Tridentine Roman printings it does carry stand on their own line and stop
before 1570. What changed is only that the Tridentine mandate, which the bull
itself cites, is now carried. The quotation supporting the new edge stands at
pustet-1862 OCR lines 158-164, with OCR damage reproduced, including `(..umque`
for `Cumque` and `Catecbismo` for `Catechismo`.

source_record.act_citation_note:
NO INSTRUMENT WAS LOCATED, AND ONE IS BELIEVED TO EXIST. A reprint described as
EMENDED was emended by someone; the 2002 book records the state and not the act.

This station is drawn because omitting it would make a postconciliar recension
silently wrong about 1971 to 1975, and the omission would be invisible: the
missal acquisition audit found this reprint by READING a leaf rather than by
searching, and recorded that a record omitting it `will be silently wrong`.

The value is `not-found` and NOT `none-claimed`, and the difference is the whole
point of having both. A `printed` station claims no act at all; this one says an
act is missing.

The date is `1971` with `date_precision = "year"`, which is what the leaf gives.
No day is invented to make it sort.
source_record.act_citation_scope:
ADDED 2026-08-01, when `check` began requiring a not-found to name what was
searched (guidance/act-histories.md section 10, item 2). The bound is stated
from what this record can support and no more.

Searched: THIS REPOSITORY'S OWN SOURCE LIBRARY, for `reimpressio`, which returns
fifteen files. They are this slice, four other inventories, one calendar, the
2008 Variationes work and its Notitiae edition, a segment record of the 2002
typical edition, and a work record for the 2008 NOTICE of the emended reprint --
that is, records ABOUT the reprint and none of the reprint's own instrument.

NOT searched: the Acta Apostolicae Sedis for 1971, Notitiae for 1971, and the
front matter of any 1971 printing. Not found here means not in the tree and not
in the witnesses this slice declares. It is not a statement about any archive.

source_record.citation: John XXIII, Rubricarum instructum, 25 July 1960, printed in the front matter of the 1962 witness.
source_record.dateline: Datum Romae, apud S. Petrum, die 25 mensis Iulii, anno 1960, Pontificatus Nostri secundo.
source_record.effect: No departure in this slice; it approves the code, which the next act promulgates.
source_record.effect_note:
This act and the one after it are two halves of one thing and are kept apart
because they are two instruments with two dates and two authorities. The motu
proprio approves the code and orders the Congregation to promulgate it; the
Congregation's decree of the following day promulgates it. Collapsing them would
lose a day, an authority and a document.
source_record.instrument: Apostolic letter motu proprio Rubricarum instructum
source_record.parent_basis:
The motu proprio names its predecessor and disposes of it: it declares that the
general Decree of the Sacred Congregation of Rites of 23 March 1955 De rubricis
ad simpliciorem formam redigendis ceases to be in force, having been taken up
into this new redaction of the rubrics. An act that says what it supersedes has
drawn its own edge.

generale S. R. C. diei 23 Martii anni 1955 l)e rubricU atl $impliciorem formam re-

source_record.effect: No departure in this slice.
source_record.effect_note:
A station that writes no row on purpose, and the third such in this history. The
constitution orders the rite of the Mass to be revised; it revises nothing
itself, and every unit that moved moved at the books the later acts promulgated.
It is carried because the constitution of 1969 states in its own title that the
Missal was restored BY DECREE OF THIS COUNCIL, so leaving it out would make the
act of 1969 look like a papal initiative standing on nothing.
source_record.instrument: Constitution on the Sacred Liturgy Sacrosanctum Concilium
source_record.parent_basis:
The state the constitution legislated for is the one the 1962 typical edition
carried: that was the missal in use when it was promulgated, eighteen months
after the edition was declared typical. Nothing in Sacrosanctum Concilium names
the 1962 edition, so the edge says where the station sits and not what it
inherited.

source_record.authority: Francis
source_record.citation: Francis, Traditionis custodes, 16 July 2021, English text on vatican.va.
source_record.dateline: Given at Rome, at Saint John Lateran, on 16 July 2021, the liturgical Memorial of Our Lady of Mount Carmel, in the ninth year of Our Pontificate. FRANCIS
source_record.effect: No departure in this file, and this station is where the line's whole point becomes visible.
source_record.effect_note:
NOTHING ON THIS LINE MOVES A TEXT, and that is why the line exists separately.
Article 1 declares the postconciliar books the unique expression of the lex
orandi of the Roman Rite; Summorum Pontificum article 1 had called the 1962
edition an extraordinary form of the same rite and said it was never abrogated.
The two are in the record, dated, quoted and NOT reconciled. No merge is drawn
between this line and the Roman one, because a merge asserts a reception and
what these documents show is the opposite.
source_record.in_force: immediately on publication in L'Osservatore Romano, by the letter's own order

permissions, and customs that do not conform to the provisions of the present

its own edge, and the nearest of those predecessors on this line is the
instruction of 2011.

crificium  omui  religionis  cultu  ac  veneratione  celebretur
[...]
decernit  sancta  synodus,  ut  ordinarii
Iocorum  episcopi  ea  omnia  prohibere  atque  e  medio  tollere
sedulo  curent  ac  teneantur,  quae  vel  avaritia,  idolorum  ser-
vitus,  vel  irreverentia,  quae  ab  impietate  vix  seiuncta  esse
potest,  vel  superstitio,  verae  pietatis  falsa  imitatrix,  induxit.
source_record.quotation_note:
Reproduced with its OCR damage (`omui` for `omni`, `Iocorum` for `locorum`,
`LEBR ATIONE` broken by the scan). The elision spans the decree's opening
argument and a running header.
source_record.root_basis:
The earliest act this file carries, and it is not offered as the beginning of
anything. What stands before it -- the mediaeval Roman curial missal, the
sacramentaries behind that, the uses out of which all of them grew -- is not
represented here and no edge is drawn into this station. A root means the record
starts here.

It is the earliest act rather than the Session XXV decree because it is the
Council's own act about the CELEBRATION OF MASS, and because the reform Quo
primum executed answers the abuses this decree names.
source_record.title: Trent orders the abuses in the celebration of Mass put down

source_record.citation: Council of Trent, Session XXV, concluded 4 December 1563, De indice librorum et catechismo, breviario et missali, in the Tauchnitz edition of 1887.
source_record.dateline: SESSIO XXV. QUAE EST NONA ET ULTIMA SUB PIO IV. PONT. MAX., COEPTA DIE III., ABSOLUTA DIE IV. DECEMBRIS MDLXIIl.
source_record.effect: Refers the missal to the Roman Pontiff. This is the act Quo primum executes, and Quo primum says so.
source_record.instrument: Decretum de indice librorum et catechismo, breviario et missali, Session XXV
source_record.locus: 1887-canones-et-decreta-tridentini OCR lines 10736-10762; the session's heading at 9021-9028
source_record.parent_basis:
Two acts of one council, in the order the council took them, and nothing in
either names the other: the Session XXV decree recites Session II, not Session
XXII. The edge says where this station sits, not what it inherited, which is
what `line-order` means and why it is the weakest kind.
source_record.quotation:
De  indice  librnrum  et  catechismo ,  breviario  et  missafi.
[...]
praecipit,  ut  quicquid  ab  illis  prae-
stitum  est  sanctissimo  Romano  Pontifici  exhibeatur,  ut  eius
iudicio  atque  auctoritate  terminetur  et  evulgetur.  Idemque
de  catechismo  a  Patribus,  quibus  illud  uiaudatuni  fuerat,
et  de  missali  et  breviario  fieri  mandat.
source_record.quotation_note:
OCR damage reproduced: `librnrum` and `missafi` in the heading, `uiaudatuni` for
`mandatum`. The operative sentence is the last: the same is ordered to be done
concerning the missal and the breviary -- that is, referred to the Roman Pontiff
for his judgement and authority, which is what Quo primum then says it is doing.

classification.classification_review_caveat: The article-page image check on 2026-10-17 establishes the scholarly description; independent altar-book collation remains open.
classification.limitations: Three selected Sanctoral preface comparisons are described by Ward; none is an independent collation of the original altar books. No immediate 1902-to-1981 whole-book succession, complete-book inheritance or first-introduction date is established. Ward distinguishes 1902 abstersit from 1954 abstulit, so the quoted 1954 predecessor must not be silently labelled 1902 wording. The Nativity-of-John preface is shortened/reordered; the Passion-of-John preface is replaced; Sebastian’s replacement is distinct from reuse of older related material as a Common-of-Martyrs collect. The source receipt and corrected transition record article-page image inspection on 2026-10-17.

classification.basis: Deri’s critical comparison identifies omission of the Pentecost-octave Mass and Transfiguration grape blessing in the Paloczi and 1484 comparators relative to the earlier Missale notatum, alongside reduced special-proper and sequence repertories. These named liturgical-content changes support the classification; relocation of preparation material is separately a book-arrangement finding.
classification.limitations: This is an aggregate endpoint change across about 150 years, not a single 1484 promulgation, an immediate parent-child edge, or proof that every omitted item ceased to be celebrated. Preparation placement concerns the book’s arrangement, not the sequence of actions during Mass.
classification.locus: p. XLIII (PDF 53); p. XLV (PDF 55); p. XLI (PDF 51)
classification.scope: Aggregate repertory and named prayer-content differences across the endpoints; not a single 1484 promulgation or immediate revision from the early witness. Preparation placement is not evidence of altered ritual order.

source_record.date_role: Title year 1543; printing completed in January 1544 new style as reported by Dubarat (28 January twice and 24 January once on p. lxxxix); original not inspected
source_record.qualification: Known here only through Dubarat's 1891 description, which reproduces the title and summarizes P. Marais's identification: the title's 'Bajocensis' is a misprint for Bayonne, corrected on folio 1 ('secundum usum ecclesie diocesis Bajon.'), and the book was ordered by Étienne Poncher, bishop of Bayonne 1532–1551 (Gallia Christiana is cited for a Bayonne missal printed under him in 1543). The Mazarine copy 1162 B was then the only one known. Not an Amiet-table record for Bayonne; the original was not inspected in this batch. The Bayonne identification is Dubarat's, after Marais, and has not been checked here against the original; Bayeux records should not absorb this book meanwhile.
source_record.source_locus: Dubarat, Le bréviaire de Lescar de 1541 (Pau, 1891), pp. lxxxix–xci (Google Books 2GkZAAAAYAAJ, PR89–PR91).
source_record.title: Missale ad usum ecclesie cathedralis [Baionensis, misprinted Bajocensis] (Paris, Jean Kaerbriand alias Huguelin for Regnault Chaudière, 1543/1544), Mazarine 1162 B

sources.inspection: Victor Dubarat, Le bréviaire de Lescar de 1541 réédité avec une introduction et des notes sur nos anciennes liturgies locales (Pau, L. Ribaut, 1891), Google Books full view. Directly viewed: p. lxxxix (identification of the 1543/1544 Paris missal titled 'Bajocensis' as Bayonne's, Poncher's order, Mazarine 1162 B as unique copy, comparison with a 1545 Bayeux missal by the same printer); p. xc (physical description, transcribed title, printer Kaerbriand alias Huguelin for Regnault Chaudière, MDXLIII, two parts of 136 and 108 folios); p. xci (calendar, blessings, temporale incipit for the diocese of Bayonne, notated prefaces including a proper Palm Sunday preface, Canon with additions, sanctoral, common and votive Masses). Pages liv and cxcviii were also viewed or OCR-read for Lescar and the later Auch-province liturgy.

The colophon names Thibaud Payen (Theobaldus Paganus) at Lyon for Jean Allard called Vandosme, bookseller of Le Puy, 1543. Lyon notes that leaf A8 is lacking in this copy. A Google Books copy (FzjRvsKsTIwC) was not inspected.

Batch 4 lane B, re-identified by cold review: this holding (BnF Vélins 201) is the copy Duine 1906 describes as no. 10 (Google Books pp. 36–37), quoting a last-leaf colophon finished at Paris on 10 January 1492 for a missal corrected by order of Bishop Michel Guibé; it is the witness of stage french-dioceses-b-batch4:rennes-1492. source_record.qualification: Exact digitized copy whose colophon dates printing to 15 February 1522 and whose preface letter (21 March 1522) describes archiepiscopal correction and chapter commissioning. The holding library dates it 1540, so it is kept separate from the catalogue witnesses iberian-zaragoza-1522 and iberian-zaragoza-1540 until edition identity is settled. Documents stage iberian-historic-batch4:zaragoza-1522 with 1522–1540 date bounds. South batch 5 (2026-10-22): the copy ends at f. CCLXXVI with final signature M (PDF pp. 600–605 re-viewed), matching the [24] + 276-leaf edition that USTC 336798 and Sánchez 224 date 1540 (as does the Zaguán record), not the [24] + CCX-leaf edition that USTC 348443 and Sánchez 109 date 1522. Its leaf count and final signature thus agree with the edition catalogued as iberian-zaragoza-1540, yet it prints a 1522 colophon; whether that edition reprints the 1522 colophon or is misdated could not be settled because CCPB and BNE refused access.

source_record.qualification: Named royal intercession at f. 48r and chapel inventories ff. 116v, 124v support a royal association, not a cathedral-wide Monza Eucharistic recension. No historical-parentage or local adoption edge is asserted.

sources.inspection: Complete PDF; title, key to manuscripts, ch. 1 Gelasian/Gregorian sections, ch. 3 selected supplement passages and manuscript bibliography. Witnesses local compilation and supplement diversity; disputed archetypes must not become universal linear reforms. Additional bounded Monza inspection on 2026-10-20: Whole Arthur Westwell, The Carolingian Sacramentaries of Saint-Amand (2024), 514 PDF pages acquired. Introduction pp. 6–7, Appendix 2 pp. 419–425 (PDF pp. 445–451), and related discussion read; Appendix 2 p. 419 visually inspected. Distinguishes treasury Berengar (called Ms.89) from F.1/101. Catalogues Mass components and later additions by folio. The date, northeastern-French manufacture and possible Cysoing/Eberhard relationship remain the author's argument, not an established Monza local-use or donor-book edge. Additional bounded Ravenna-fragment inspection on 2026-10-20: Whole book PDF acquired from institutional repository; title/rights page, p. 42, note 121 / PDF p. 68, 56 note 180, 58-62 and note 201 inspected. Discusses Montecassino 271 as a mass-prayer/reading book, the single Stockholm-Wroclaw codex, and the evidential limits of Gamber's Ravenna archetype hypothesis. LIMIT: Critical discussion does not independently date or locate the fragment scriptoria. No Ravenna archetype is promoted to a surviving book or historical stage. PDF figures carry separate rights.
sources.label: Arthur Westwell, The Carolingian Sacramentaries of Saint-Amand (2024)
