source_record.date: 680–691 per ELMSS 648, USUARIUM and the IA catalogue note (written, or copied from a book written, under Abbot Cronan of Bangor, County Down)
source_record.qualification: One Irish manuscript from Bangor, County Down. USUARIUM records it twice (book 1025, origin 'Bangor, County Down'; book 6091, origin 'Bangor', whose own remark places the monastery in Down) and the Gamber index has matching rows 150 and 1968:0150; merged here as one manuscript identity, not a Welsh Bangor book. Predominantly an Office book (canticles, hymns, collects and anthems for the hours). Its Eucharistic material is limited to identifiable items: the communion hymn 'Hymnus quando communicant sacerdotes', 'Ad pacem celebrandam', collects/anthems 'Ad communionem', and the anthems Warren numbers [109]–[115] and calls Eucharistic. It contains no Mass order or sacramentary. Folio loci of the Eucharistic items not checked against the facsimile (HBS 4); identification rests on Warren's 1895 contents and introduction in uncorrected OCR. Edition date: USUARIUM 1025 and IA metadata give 1893 for part II, but the part II OCR title block reads 1895; part I is catalogued as 1893 (IA metadata, title page not checked). ELMSS 648 (CLA 3.311, fetched by the cold reviewer on 2026-10-19) dates the book VII ex (680–691), written at Bangor during the abbacy recorded in the hymn on its last page; ELMSS names that abbot Colman, whereas USUARIUM and the edition tradition name Cronan. The coordinate follows ELMSS.

source_record.qualification: Sedda Anthony Mass scheme I (Os iusti), shared with Napoli VI.G.38. A central-Italian Minorite missal copied from a pre-Haymonian antigraph (before 1244), later owned by Cardinal Bessarion. Fascicle XIX (ff. 190–194) is a later addition supplying feasts introduced in the fourteenth century (Trinity, Holy Cross, Holy Spirit, three Marian Masses, Stabat mater) and is a separate layer. Welch 2011 queries its Franciscan identity. Named state/witness retained; no full original collation or continuous genealogy claimed.

source_record.qualification: This undertext is the libellus of Gallican Masses edited by Mone (1850) and known as the Mone Masses: Suski 2022, entry [47], identifies these Aug. 253 folios as a libellus missarum gallicanus (Missae Mone), VII (630–640), France (Burgundy), CLLA 203, CLA VIII 1102, which is ELMSS 1569. Suski's narrower 630–640 is attributed; the coordinate follows ELMSS VII. Distinct from the other Aug. 253 undertexts (ELMSS 1567, 1568, 1570). The number of Masses and their relation to other Gallican books are not collated here; the retained Mone 1850 scan has no usable text layer. Host BLB PDF is the 372-page Aug. 253 codex, not a complete missal; this candidate links only its ELMSS 1569 bounded folio segment. No legible undertext transcription or textual collation is claimed.

source_record.qualification: ELMSS 715: a Gregorian sacramentary written doubtless in Italy in a neat later-type uncial, erased and rewritten with Gregory's Dialogi in the Beneventan zone in the eleventh century. A Gregorian book copied around 700 witnesses the Gregorian tradition before the Hadrianum reached Francia; its exact Mass components and its relation to the Hadrianum and to the pre-Hadrianic witnesses (Trent 1590, the Clm 6333 layers) are unresolved. Kept in this lane because the packet's use latin-early-use-roman-sacramentary-fragments-italy names it as a Roman-type fragment and the Italian lane's files in this pass hold no record for it. Copying date only.

Additional bounded Ravenna-fragment inspection on 2026-10-20: Exact lower-layer identification, VII–VIII (680-720) date, Gregorian sacramentary-fragment contents and Italian origin inspected. Provenance identifies eleventh-century Beneventan rewriting with Gregory's Dialogues. Complete catalogue illustration of p. 84 inspected. source_record.title: Kroměříž, Arcidiecézní muzeum, inv. RKP 21134 (sign. O / c V 1): pre-Hadrianic Gregorian sacramentary

sources.inspection: Complete PDF; title, key to manuscripts, ch. 1 Gelasian/Gregorian sections, ch. 3 selected supplement passages and manuscript bibliography. Witnesses local compilation and supplement diversity; disputed archetypes must not become universal linear reforms. Additional bounded Monza inspection on 2026-10-20: Whole Arthur Westwell, The Carolingian Sacramentaries of Saint-Amand (2024), 514 PDF pages acquired. Introduction pp. 6–7, Appendix 2 pp. 419–425 (PDF pp. 445–451), and related discussion read; Appendix 2 p. 419 visually inspected. Distinguishes treasury Berengar (called Ms.89) from F.1/101. Catalogues Mass components and later additions by folio. The date, northeastern-French manufacture and possible Cysoing/Eberhard relationship remain the author's argument, not an established Monza local-use or donor-book edge. Additional bounded Ravenna-fragment inspection on 2026-10-20: Whole book PDF acquired from institutional repository; title/rights page, p. 42, note 121 / PDF p. 68, 56 note 180, 58-62 and note 201 inspected. Discusses Montecassino 271 as a mass-prayer/reading book, the single Stockholm-Wroclaw codex, and the evidential limits of Gamber's Ravenna archetype hypothesis. LIMIT: Critical discussion does not independently date or locate the fragment scriptoria. No Ravenna archetype is promoted to a surviving book or historical stage. PDF figures carry separate rights.

source_record.chronology_certainty: 1555 author/year from afterword per BKSH; exact day from retrospective Vatican News; printing year attributed, not separately proved
source_record.date_role: reported colophon completion 5 January 1555; bracketed printing year from afterword
source_record.qualification: The national catalogue identifies a facsimile of the incomplete Vatican-held exemplar, with lost title leaf and other missing leaves represented by blanks. The closing statement is reported to date composition from 20 March 1554 to 5 January 1555; [1555] printing is catalogued from the afterword, while place and printer are unknown. The book mixes Mass, sacramental, biblical, devotional and catechetical material. Vatican News 2026 describes it as chiefly translated, with some original Albanian material. The BKSH record separately reports an undated handwritten Italian note attributing a Latin source; no Latin exemplar or textual relation has been directly compared. Priest use is retrospectively reported, but approval, operative jurisdiction, exact contents and relation to Latin exemplars are unverified. This witness does not establish a distinct Roman source recension or act-history station.
source_record.source_locus: BKSH record 92035 notes on date, Vatican exemplar and missing leaves; Vatican News 2026 opening and contents paragraphs; Chiaramonte 2020 Status quaestionis/Libri-mit; BnF Ressuli 1958 facsimile Comprend field; TITUS part 1 editorial note/page 009r; USUARIUM origin 1153 saved book 9559.

source_record.qualification: The separately sourced Si quid est act dates Urban VIII approval to 1634. Torra Miró p. 188 no. 120 lists a UB Rome 1634 Typographia Vaticana/Andrea Brogiotto missal; UB Alma MMS 991002308499706708 is a strong likely match, not an explicit item crosswalk. Its supplied [Missale Romanum] title and bracketed [Roma : Andrea Brogiotto : Typographia Vaticana, 1634?] imprint are catalogue metadata; the probable imprint is said to derive from preliminaries without identifying a dated leaf. The reported [51], 563, XCV, [3] pages and [11] illustrations do not establish completeness: the held copy lacks its title page and Q1 and binds a separate 1764 addition. Original-book images and 1634/1635 text collation remain unacquired. Batch 3 official CCPB record CCPB000821832-3 and copy CCPH002069693-0 support a crosswalk to this same defective UB holding and explicitly identify 86/3/20 as its shelfmark. CCPB leaves the main publication unknown and puts probable Rome/Brogiotto/Vaticana 1634 in a preliminary-matter note; the fingerprint also questions 1634. Exact setting controls and bounded current BiPaDi searches are recorded in the new follow-up receipt. The questioned imprint, complete original extent and absence of a directly inspected original remain unresolved.

source_record.date_role: imprint-and-colophon-year; witness to the 1634 approval-stage recension
source_record.qualification: Exact digitized original copy of a Rome Vatican 1635 printing whose title states recognition 'nunc denuo' by Urban VIII and carries no edition statement. Title and colophon both read MDCXXXV. The book prints Quo primum, Cum sanctissimum, Si quid est (dated 2 September 1634) and a Congregation of Rites decree extract that Urban VIII ordered placed in the Missal then to be printed. Register: †-†††† (56 pp.), A-Z, Aa-Zz, Aaa-Bbb, a-h; page sequence consistent with SBN UM1E008100 ([56], 572, XCVII, [3]), not with the Secunda editio [40], 444, LXXVI settings. It witnesses the Urbanian recension stage roman-stages-1634; it is not a 1634-dated imprint, and its relation to UB's defective [1634?] copy, to any 1634 issue and to the 1635 Secunda editio is unresolved. No body-text collation outside the strict Canon (printed pp. 245-249), which is transcribed and independently collated as a bounded constituent bound to roman-stages-1634.

sources.inspection: Viewed 2026-10-21 (page images): PP7 title Romae, Ex Typographia Vaticana, MDCXXXV, De licentia superiorum, no edition statement, manuscript 'Balth. Moreti'; PP9 Quo primum; PP10 Cum sanctissimum (7 July 1604); PP11-PP12 Si quid est (sig. †3; Andrea Brogiotto named; dated 2 September 1634); PP12 Congregation of Rites decree extract ordered for the new Missal printing; PP13 De anno (sig. †4); PT3 saints' index; PT4 Regestum (†-††††, A-Z, Aa-Zz, Aaa-Bbb, a-h) and colophon MDCXXXV. Google page sequence: 62 preliminary, 572 arabic, 96 roman, 8 terminal images.

source_record.qualification: Rusca Lanzada L-77 (printed p. 49) catalogues a Rome Vatican 1635 'Secunda editio' with saints' proper Masses set out at length; its copy is incomplete after p. 4 of the final sequence. Asachiana 19 (2023), printed pp. 15-16, photographs another Rome Vatican 1635 title leaf and describes a defective/composite copy, but its stated 698-page complete extent does not reconcile with its section breakdown. Whether these are the same or different settings/issues, or whether either changes the 1634 text substantively, is unverified. Bibliographic witness lead only; no new stage. SBN adds Rome Vatican bibliographic records for explicitly Secunda editio (UM1E041839: [40],444,LXXVI), Tertia editio (PBEE017510: [40],448,LXXVI,[4]), and a larger setting without a transcribed edition label (UM1E008100: catalogue displays [56!,572,XCVII,[3! pages). Preserve them as distinct setting/issue leads until original title and collation verify identity. No new recension/station or 1634/1635 parentage.

Forty original native DjVu pages 237–276 and the index retain source/context evidence; the selected facsimile has 18 pages. These 52 units and the separate offertory are complete declared constituents, not a complete Ordinary or Missal. On 20 October 2026 a separate complete functional Pater constituent was independently source-read in both printed chant forms, from Orémus on FIDES raw 0275 / printed 213 to final Amén. on raw 0277 / printed 215 left, before Deinde/Libera. Its eight units preserve fifteen source blocks over three complete-page witness images; final Amén. remains an independently preferred probable acute at a crease/worn area, with an explicit source-condition reservation. Wider post-Canon text through raw 0285 / printed 219 remains blocked by concealed letters and punctuation at raw 0278, 0281 and 0282. Context raw 0286 is a Resurrection engraving and raw 0287 / printed 221 opens Dominica Resurrectionis. The repeated printed 214–217 labels retain offered file order; their physical cause is unestablished. The title-confirmed Google/Lyon1657 alternate has different typesetting and supplies no concealed readings. Earlier offertory 25 and Canon 52, partial whole-book status and unknown textual parents remain unchanged. On 2026-10-21 the March calendar page-file 0025 (FIDES raw page 25, from the previously acquired native DjVu) was rendered locally and inspected.

sources.inspection: Complete University of Ottawa digitization acquired 2026-10-22 (32,313,093 bytes). Introduction pp. 12*, 17* and 18* (PDF 16, 21, 22) read as page images: plenary missal of Romano-Frankish liturgy, beginning lost up to the Christmas Vigil, Preface and Canon at the Easter Vigil (f. 80); no title, colophon or calendar; dated by script and notation to the early eleventh century, earlier authors having proposed the late tenth; Communicantes adds Hilary, Martin, Jerome, Ambrose, Augustine, Gregory, Benedict and Isidore; the Pater embolism names Bartholomew after Peter, Paul and Andrew; the editors conclude Beneventan origin in the early eleventh century, probably for a Benedictine monastery, with long later use shown by corrections. Facsimile plates ff. 80r–81r (PDF 231–233) viewed by the research fork.
sources.limitations: Modern critical facsimile, copyright Peter Lang; loci cited only. The archive.org metadata mislabels the year as 1889. sources.inspection: Page images of printed pp. 359–360 (PDF 33–34) viewed 2026-10-22 from a prior-lane copy of the whole issue (SHA-256 f31becd3…). Under section III (Decreta circa ritus et calendaria particularia) the Order of Preachers is granted, for the whole Order, the restored Missale Romanum of Paul VI and the Universal Norms with the new General Roman Calendar and Litany; after adoption the Master General (for the Order) or a provincial (for his subjects) may license priests to celebrate according to the Dominican rite then in force; until a definitive Order calendar is approved, first-class Dominican feasts (Rosary, Dominic, Thomas Aquinas, Catherine of Siena) become solemnities, second-class feasts become feasts, third-class saints obligatory memorials and the rest optional memorials. A following paragraph gives pastoral reasons and the difficulty of printing proper books for this and a Cistercian request.
sources.limitations: Published decree summary, not the signed rescript or its ASOP 39 (1969) pp. 250–251 printing. It grants permission; it does not date the Order's actual changeover or any house's licensed continuation of the Dominican rite.

sources.inspection: Page images of printed pp. 14, 17 and 18 (PDF 20, 27–28) viewed 2026-10-22 (copy SHA-256 0ccd64a2…). sources.inspection: Canvases 1–24 surveyed as thumbnails; canvas 7 (printed mandate) and canvas 8 (January calendar) read at full size, 2026-10-22. The mandate of Ernst, archbishop of Magdeburg and administrator of the church of Halberstadt, to the clergy of the city and diocese of Halberstadt says that the missals in use vary among themselves and depart from the true rubric, and that he has therefore granted missals to be printed according to the order and true rubric of Halberstadt from the most corrected exemplars, urging churches to buy them; it ends 'Datum Halberstadt' without a date. Calendar canvases 8–19.
sources.limitations: No colophon was read; the date ca. 1498 and the printer are the BSB/GW attribution (the BSB note also cites Fuchs ca. 1493–1500, BM STC 1500? and Proctor's sixteenth-century placing). Body uncollated.

sources.inspection: Canvases 1–24 and 520–543 surveyed as thumbnails; canvas 5 (title), canvas 7 (January calendar) and canvas 534 (address Ad clerum Halberstattensem) read at full size, 2026-10-22. A second MDZ object, bsb10942166, describes the same BSB copy.
sources.limitations: Printer and place are catalogue attributions; Mass bodies and other calendar months are uncollated.

evidence.claim: Identifies Catholic Patriarchate publication in 1898 and a modified re-edition of Tuki’s 1736 text.

The 1898 Coptic Catholic synod lists the Euchologium seu Missale as containing the three Alexandrian anaphoras preceded by the evening and morning incense offices, with the Katameros, hymn book, Synaxarium and homilies as complements, and requires every edition of the liturgical books to conform to the most ancient exemplars and to those approved by the Apostolic See.
evidence.locus: Sectio II cap. I art. II n. 4(a) and n. 5, pp. 52–53

evidence.claim: Only the three anaphoras (that ascribed to Mark and said to be arranged by Cyril, Basil and Gregory Nazianzen) may be used; Basil is customary on ordinary days and lesser feasts and Gregory on greater feasts of the Lord, and Mark is commended for his feast and fast days; no priest may celebrate without the printed exemplar before him; the Roman custom of joining thumb and forefinger after the consecration of the bread is stated as already in force; clergy genuflect after each consecration and before the fraction.
evidence.locus: Sectio II cap. III art. IV secunda pars I, canons I–III, VII and XIII, pp. 105–108

evidence.claim: The words of institution are declared the form of consecration; the Spirit invocation of the Alexandrian Basil liturgy is quoted in Latin and interpreted as presupposing a consecration already made; the canons require adoration after each consecration and the invocation to be said with head deeply bowed while ministers and people remain in adoration.
evidence.locus: Sectio II cap. III art. IV prima pars V, pp. 90–92

evidence.claim: Dates the synod (18 January–3 June 1898) and its Roman recognition (examined 27 February 1899, approved in papal audience 23 April 1899, decree 1 May 1899).

Addendum 2026-10-22: the 1898 synod acts (an inspected primary act) now fix the normative frame of the Catholic Euchologion in the same year: the three-anaphora repertoire with the incense offices, conformity to ancient and Apostolic-See-approved exemplars, a printed exemplar at every celebration, and adoration rubrics at the consecration and the Spirit invocation. They do not mention the 1898 printing or the relocation of the intercession, so they neither date nor confirm Lietzmann's description; the book itself remains unlocated (see the gap row).
stages.reception: Chaîne identifies the Catholic Patriarchate as publisher; Hammerschmidt independently lists this as a Catholic edition. Dates of actual local adoption are not established. The 1898 synod of the Coptic Catholic hierarchy, recognized at Rome in 1899, makes the printed Euchologion obligatory at every celebration and limits use to its three anaphoras; parish-level adoption dates of the 1898 printing remain unestablished.
stages.scope: Coptic-Arabic Euchologion and placement of the intercession relative to its anaphoras.

stages.limitations: Section headings and paratext only; the Ge’ez prayers are not transcribed or compared with UM-039, later manuscripts or the Catholic printings. Only the INTROITVS MISSE heading was read at f. 158r; identifying ff. 158r–167v as the Ordo communis with the anaphora of the Apostles follows Hammerschmidt (inventory source geez-hammerschmidt-anaphoras-preview), not a heading on the page. Addendum 2026-10-22: Mercer (1915, p. 146) attributes Catholic-oriented alterations to the printed text (omitted Monophysite names, Filioque in the Creed, an altered Invocation); these are recorded as his scholarly description only, because the corresponding 1548 pages were not read.

Mercer (1915) describes the text as prepared for the Uniates; that is an attribution of editorial intent, not evidence of use by a Catholic community.

stages.limitations: Printer differs from Sabbio-labelled catalogue leads; use exact shelfmark and resolve before acquisition. No claim 1594 was the first effective removal. The 1640 edition, directly inspected, lacks the Veronica proper, which is consistent with but does not verify the 1594 removal. The 1609 letter (ambrosian-1609) says that Archbishop Gaspar (Visconti) had the missal emended, printed and promulgated and that Federico kept the changes of the latest, commonly received edition; it names no year, so it does not itself date that edition to 1594. On 4 February the calendar has the Chair of Peter at Antioch, and the Sanctoral passes from Blaise to that Chair by referral and then to Agatha, with no Veronica Mass.

The Google (Angelica) copy is bibliography entry 103. FSL A/711 (EAP) is a mixed copy whose title, pp. 1–6 and corrections share entry 103's settings while pp. 7–19 are reset; at the Creed the reset pages agree with entry 103, so no distinct state is shown there. Cold review 2026-10-22: the EAP copy is not attached as a witness of this stage, because its reset pp. 7–19 carry the anaphora and most of the ordinary, are compared only at the Creed, and are of unknown date and printer; this keeps the 2026-10-20 decision that the copy needs its own approval before stage admission. Entry 104 (50 continuous pages, type area 24 × 16 cm, four woodcuts) is known only from the bibliography, which reports Zarbhanalian's and Ghazikian's view that it was printed much later; no copy has been inspected, and the EAP reset pages cannot be assigned to it (they carry no woodcut and the attached corrections keep entry 103's numbering 21–30). Whether the reset or entry 104 is a later impression is unresolved. Whole-book verbal collation remains incomplete.

stages.label: Patriarchal Armenian Catholic service book issued for episcopal examination
stages.limitations: The retained scan lacks the 174-page celebrant’s order, so the ordinary’s text and its textual family rest on the retrospective. The declaration presents the book as an examination exemplar; no synodal decision or Roman confirmation of it has been inspected. No 1677-to-1879 revision edge is asserted. Cold review 2026-10-21: the 1904 Vienna printing is recorded here as a later witness of this state, not as a separate station, because its only inspected warrant is a permission for a second printing of the 1879 book without change of the text (except with the patriarch’s consent); no page collation of 1879 and 1904 has been made, and only lections were seen in the 1904 copy. Addendum 2026-10-22: the lection for the fourth day of Epiphany (p. 19) prints the heavenly-witnesses clause of 1 John 5:7; whether earlier Armenian Catholic lection books did so on that day is not compared here, so no lectionary transition is asserted.
stages.reception: Explicitly a patriarchal Armenian Catholic publication, issued for episcopal examination. The patriarch authorized a second printing in 1903 (Vienna 1904), which the 1951 Enciclopedia Cattolica names as the plenary book in Armenian Catholic use (inventory note, not independently verified here).

stages.reception: The book is addressed to Benedictine professors throughout Germany and assigned to the Bursfelde observance. This BSB copy carries undated manuscript Mass-proper supplements for saints venerated at Trier (among them Eucharius, Valerius, Maternus, Agritius, Celsus and Matthias, including an Electio sancti Mathie entry and a Matthias sequence), which show local supplementation in one copy; the house and date of use are not identified.

stages.summary: The title calls the book newly and most diligently corrected and revised for the reformed black monks of Bursfelde. The printer's recognitor says the order's missals had been carefully emended by Johannes Trithemius in orthography and accents but had since become corrupted by copyists, and that this edition expunges those faults; the colophon calls its exemplar newly emended and corrected in many places by a religious of the order. The inspected Canon units and the January feast entries agree in content with the 1498 printing; the January golden numbers differ.

Upgrading still requires a demonstrated textual difference from the Ratdolt 1510 edition.
stages.reception: No reception evidence.

evidence.claim: The manuscript is indexed as a gradual and missal with a Roman-curial order title and Mass components in Franciscan Zadar context.

Which Roman printing Renaudot meant (before 1716; possibly the Maronite 'Missale Chaldaicum' of 1592/1594) is not established. No continuity with the 1767 Propaganda edition is asserted.
stages.reception: A copy by the Catholic patriarch at Rome attests a Catholic editorial state; local use of the copy is not established.
stages.scope: One Catholic East Syriac manuscript state of the Apostles' anaphora, known only through Renaudot's note at the consignation and fraction.
stages.summary: Renaudot's base codex (the codex of Elias) lacks the whole recitation of Christ's words at the consignation before the fraction. He reports that in the copy Patriarch Joseph wrote at Rome in 1697 that entire locus was reformed after the Missale Chaldaicum printed at Rome, as in the Mass whose version Alexis de Menezes published; a marginal note places a prayer after the dominical words in a more recent codex.
stages.witness_label: Manuscript written at Rome in 1697 by Joseph, Chaldean patriarch, as described by Renaudot (1716); shelfmark not given

evidence.claim: The Roman edition of 1767 excluded the second and third anaphoras, and in its anaphora of the Apostles the double consecration of bread and wine was placed at the beginning of the fraction rite.
The Propaganda missal printed in 1767 contained only the first (Apostles) liturgy; by 1885 the edition was exhausted.

stages.label: Rome: Catholic Propaganda missal recension
stages.limitations: Only the titles and selected anaphoral pages have been checked. No claim of first Catholic printing or complete list of Latin/Maronite additions. Institution placement at the fraction still requires a precise comparison. Addendum 2026-10-22: Delly (1957, p. 164) describes the 1767 Apostles anaphora as printing the double consecration at the start of the fraction, and Delly (p. 162 n. 2) and Vosté (1945, p. 68) report that the book omitted the second and third anaphoras; Vosté does not describe the consecration placement; the exact 1767 page of the displaced consecration has not been located on the low-resolution scan, so this remains a scholarly description.
stages.reception: Publication by the Roman Propaganda Congregation identifies a Catholic book; breadth and continuity of local adoption not independently established.
stages.scope: Catholic printed witness; bounded Addai and Mari readings established through the critical apparatus, full ordinary not yet inspected.
stages.summary: The original Propaganda title identifies a Catholic printed state. In the Addai and Mari intercession, printed p. 284 omits the life-giving Gospel phrase that the Mosul 1901 printed p. 35 includes.
stages.witness_label: Missale Chaldaicum ex decreto Sacrae Congregationis de Propaganda Fide editum (Rome, 1767)

evidence.claim: Native beginning and 1901 imprimatur inspected.
Complementary proper volume shares the 1901 Mosul Dominican imprint.
Specifies 1901 pp. 24–36 as Cm 01 and records the relevant anaphoral readings.
evidence.locus: p. 357 Cm 01; p. 363 note 10; p. 366 line 53 apparatus

evidence.claim: Native intercession directly checked against Rome 1767 printed p. 284/PDF 339.

From Propaganda archive letters: the text was revised by Patriarch Khayyat's commission and the bishops; Propaganda had it printed by the Mosul Dominicans at its own expense while expressly granting no direct or indirect approval (letters of 18 September 1896 and 22 August 1901); printing was suspended after Khayyat's death on 6 November 1899 amid episcopal dispute over the text and over rubrics added by Joseph Khayyat; publication was announced on 21 March 1902.
The Mosul Dominican missal contains the three liturgies; the lections, the missal for the dead and the baptism and marriage ritual were issued separately.

stages.label: Mosul: ordinary and complementary propers
stages.limitations: The companion volume is not a second stage. 1901 attests these readings; it does not date their introduction. Macomber also finds the post-Sanctus insertion in a late nineteenth-century Mar Ya‘qob ritual. Addendum 2026-10-22: Delly reports that the Chaldean synod's approval was conditional on a revision by two bishops that, according to the Apostolic Delegation, was not carried out, and that Propaganda authorized printing without approving the text; the restoration of the second and third anaphoras relative to 1767 is source-described, not collated here.
stages.reception: Catholic imprimatur from Henricus Altmayer, Apostolic Delegate, 22 October 1901. It authorizes printing; it does not establish universal use or an independent complete reform. Delly (p. 170) reports opposition from Archbishop Thomas Audo of Urmia, who issued his own 1906 missal, and states that the 1901 book, reprinted in 1936 at the patriarchal press in Mosul, was in use in all Chaldean dioceses including Persia by 1957.
stages.scope: One publication state represented by complementary ordinary/anaphoral and temporal-sanctoral proper volumes.
stages.summary: The ordinary prints the expanded Lord’s Prayer near the beginning and the life-giving Gospel phrase in the Addai and Mari intercession. Macomber locates the institution narrative at the opening of the post-Sanctus prayer.
stages.witness_label: Missale juxta ritum Ecclesiae Syrorum Orientalium, id est Chaldaeorum; companion Proprium missarum de tempore et de sanctis (Mosul, Dominican press, 1901)

evidence.claim: Syriac and Latin title Missale Chaldaicum with the date 1906.
Collation statement concordat cum Missali impresso Romae anno 1767 signed by Thomas Audo, archbishop of the Chaldeans of Urmia, and nihil obstat of Franciscus Lesné, Apostolic Delegate in Persia.
States the integration of Epistles, Gospels and proper chants, the 1767 ordinary as followed at Urmia and Salmas, and the absence of any claim to impose the book on the Chaldean Church.
Independently identifies the 1906 Urmia missal as Thomas Audo's, issued in opposition to the 1901 Mosul missal, and quotes the same preface.

stages.label: Urmia: Archbishop Thomas Audo's missal with integrated propers
stages.limitations: The body of the book (245 pages) was not read or collated: neither the agreement of its ordinary with 1767 nor the content of its propers is checked here. The approbation leaf is undated; 1906 is the title-page year. The preface's statement about earlier missals concerns the books then used in Urmia parishes and is the editor's description.
stages.reception: Issued by the Catholic archbishop of Urmia with the Apostolic Delegate's nihil obstat for the parishes of Urmia and Salmas, not as a patriarchal or synodal book for the whole Chaldean Church; Delly (1957) judges the opposition it expressed short-lived. No date of local adoption or abandonment is established.
stages.scope: Chaldean Catholic missal printed at the Lazarist press in Urmia for the Urmia and Salmas parishes: the Rome 1767 ordinary with the Sunday and feast Epistles and Gospels and the proper chants placed in the same volume.
stages.summary: The approbation leaf carries Archbishop Thomas Audo of Urmia's attestation that, after careful collation, the book agrees with the missal printed at Rome in 1767, and the nihil obstat of Franciscus Lesné, Apostolic Delegate in Persia. The French preface says that earlier missals held only the ordinary, so that the Epistles and Gospels (in two separate manuscript books) and the introit, pre-Epistle verse, gradual, offertory and communion (in the Hudra and Gazza) had to be sought in four books; this missal places all of them in one volume, with only references for the psalms and the optional Old Testament lessons. It takes the 1767 ordinary as followed at Urmia and Salmas, rejects the unfixed Mesopotamian deviations, and disclaims any intention of imposing a new missal on the Chaldean Church.
stages.witness_label: Taksā kaldāyā / Missale Chaldaicum (Urmia: Lazarist Fathers' press, 1906), 11, 245 pp.; ULB Bonn 3058506

evidence.claim: Reports 2005 synod, 18 February 2006 recognitio, and 6 January 2007 implementation date.

stages.reception: Jammo states St Peter’s diocese would implement. Sako later disputes wider acceptance and whether the printed text included synodal corrections; these accounts are not collapsed into universal reception.
stages.scope: Identifiable reform described by its compiler and scholarly observer; text identity and reception distinguished.
stages.summary: The reform places the institution narrative after the intercessions, before the epiclesis/anamnesis sequence, and directs audible anaphoral recitation. Royel also describes removal of diaconal exhortations around the Pax.
stages.witness_label: Reformed Takhsa d-Raze, approved 2005/recognized 2006 according to Jammo; original Syriac edition still to acquire

The 2025 reprint's instructions (printed iii–iv) differ in detail from 2020 PDF 3–4: an entrance-chant alternative noting the absence of a sanctuary curtain, an added alternative epiclesis chant, sixteen numbered items instead of fifteen, and an introduction no longer naming Sureth and English. These are recorded as reprint corrections, not a separately approved revision.

The 1486 mandate is a separate event from 1487 publication; the date of first introduction of individual clauses is unestablished. Retained source images and bounded readings do not provide a checked canonical text transcription.

stages.scope: Printed order missal prepared under the 1486 commission for uniform corrected liturgical books.
stages.summary: The opening mandate of Johannes abbot of Cîteaux orders corrected missals, breviaries and psalters under general-chapter authority and directs houses to acquire and conform their books. The colophon dates this printing to 4 September 1487. Its Memento lacks two clauses found in 1606, while both Canon openings retain the king among named intercessions.
stages.witness_label: Missale Cisterciense, Strasbourg, Johann Grüninger, 1487; BSB 2 Inc.c.a. 1921, bsb 00044164; USUARIUM 423

evidence.claim: Explicit reforms of the 1601 and 1605 chapters; full conformity in the Canon, limited conformity elsewhere.
Three bounded prayer units directly transcribed from page images.

Complete bounded offertory constituent independently collated, including all intervening rubrics and response cues. The literal binding and extent census remain separate from partial whole-book text coverage.

Complete declared Canon constituent independently collated in 35 ordered units, including five seasonal Communicantes forms, Easter/Pentecost Hanc igitur and rubrics; excludes the following Oremus and Pater noster. Whole-book coverage remains partial.
evidence.locus: Canon printed sequence 190–197 (fourth page misnumbered 192); BSB canvases 244–251; provider PDF 245–252

evidence.claim: The separate complete bounded post-Canon tail and appended Suffragium are independently collated in 64 source-order units: Orémus/Præcéptis after the excluded strict Canon final Amen on printed p. 197, the main Order closure on p. 199, and the p. 200 Suffragium through final Amen before Sanctorale p. 201. The appendix is physically printed after the main closure but its own rubric assigns recitation after Pater noster Canonis; it is retained in physical source order. A five-page lossless facsimile retains printed pp. 197–201, with p. 201 outside the constituent as boundary evidence. Earlier offertory and Canon IDs and literal bytes remain unchanged. This complete bounded composite selection does not complete the Ordinary or whole Missal, imply uninterrupted printed chapter divisions, establish monastery reception or supply ancestry.
evidence.locus: Printed pp. 197–200; BSB canvases 251–254; provider PDF 252–255; p. 201 boundary context retained separately

evidence.claim: Printed March entries: Albinus (1), Thomas Aquinas (7), Gregory (12), Cuthbert as an English commemoration (20), Benedict (21) and Annuntiatio Dominica (25), graded by lessons and Masses; the 19 March line is printed blank in both BSB copies.
evidence.locus: March calendar, BSB canvas 17; control copy bsb10496384 canvas 17

stages.label: 1606 Romanizing Cistercian missal
stages.limitations: This is already a revised state, not a proxy for all medieval Cistercian practice. The exact 1606 witness has now been split from the earlier broad printed-witness cluster. No claim that every decree of 1601 or 1605 was fully received locally.
stages.reception: The book identifies itself as for the Cistercian Order and invokes chapter authority; no monastery-by-monastery reception census has been made. In BSB 2 Liturg. 205 a a later hand added in red ink at 19 March Iosephi Christi Nutritoris, twelve lessons, one Mass; the second copy 2 Liturg. 207 a has no such addition. The addition is undated copy-level evidence of local calendar supplementation.
stages.scope: Printed order missal implementing Roman conformity in the Canon while retaining Cistercian usages elsewhere.
stages.summary: The 1606 Annotanda attributes full Roman conformity in the Canon to the 1601 and 1605 general chapters, and conformity elsewhere only as proper Cistercian use allows. The printed Ordinary still has a short Confiteor, a combined Suscipe Trinitas offering, and Orate/Dominus sit response.

Primary description of the new revision; retained graduals prevent complete Roman imitation.
Three complete paired prayers and their position in the offertory read from images.

Complete bounded offertory constituent independently collated, including all intervening rubrics and response cues. The literal binding and extent census remain separate from partial whole-book text coverage.

Complete declared Canon constituent independently collated in 52 ordered units: 19 prefatory heading/prayer/rubric units and 33 title/main units. The final Amen and Iungit manus precede excluded Oremus/Pater; other preface text is excluded. Different placement of seasonal forms does not establish their abolition, and whole-book coverage remains partial.

stages.label: 1657 further Roman correction
stages.limitations: The 1651 commission, 1655 mandate, and 1657 publication are distinct dates. The inspected 1655 instrument is not a universal effective-date decree. The Monitum historical catalogue of earlier defects must not all be assigned specifically to 1606.
stages.reception: The Cistercian superior authorizes the edition and printing monopoly; this is evidence of intended order use, not uniform local implementation.
stages.scope: Printed Cistercian missal following the 1651 commission; a substantially Romanized Ordinary while retaining order-specific material.
stages.summary: The Ordinary enlarges the Confiteor with named saints including Bernard and triple culpa; replaces the old Orate and response; prints separate host and chalice offerings and a revised Suscipe Trinitas after Lavabo. The Monitum reports reordered Pentecost-to-Advent Sunday Masses and Roman rubrics, but expressly retains differences in the graduals.

text_projections.title: Cistercian missal 1657: complete bounded offertory constituent
Cistercian missal 1657: Canon with its prefatory proper forms
Cistercian missal 1657: Pater noster in its two chant forms

stages.label: Verona collection of Roman sacramentary prayers
stages.limitations: The 551–600 coordinate is a palaeographic copying range, not the composition of the libelli or a date of Roman promulgation. The collection is not shown to be a complete missal or a public-service exemplar; no folio-level text checked.
stages.reception: The catalogue reports a later Verona connection, not evidence that this codex or collection was universally received in Rome.
stages.scope: Verona Biblioteca Capitolare LXXXV (80), the surviving collection of sacramentary material; seventh-century continuation distinguished from the core.

stages.label: Old Gelasian manuscript in two present holdings
stages.limitations: The year bounds now span both catalogue datings (BAV 'Sec. VIII in.'; ELMSS VIII med., 726–775); neither is adopted over the other. The Paris appendix leaves were not image-checked (Gallica HTTP 403). Neither Pope Gelasius's authorship, the date of individual prayers, nor direct descent into later Gelasian books follows from this witness. Wilson's 1894 critical edition is not an ancient stage.
stages.reception: Surviving Frankish manuscript evidence; no universal Roman institution or continuous use period is inferred.
stages.scope: The surviving sacramentary Reg. lat. 316 and its detached Paris appendix, not a complete reconstruction of earlier text strata.
stages.summary: The catalogue treats the Vatican and Paris portions as one eighth-century codex with sacramentary, exorcism and penitential contents. Original images confirm the incipit naming a liber sacramentorum Romanae aecclesiae ordinis anni circuli (f. 4r), a decorated opening of Book II for the saints (f. 132r) and the explicit of the Vatican volume (f. 245r).
stages.witness_label: Vatican Reg. lat. 316 with Paris BnF lat. 7193 ff. 41–56

evidence.claim: Identifies the copy date, mixed sacramentary character and a ninth-century addition at f. 1.
evidence.locus: Date; Description, contents and f. 1 addition

stages.label: Gellone sacramentary manuscript
stages.limitations: The codex's physical extent is not a checked transcription or a complete reconstructed missal. The 1981 edition is modern scholarship. The catalogue's mixed-text description establishes neither exact donor books nor an archetype for other Frankish Gelasian witnesses.
stages.reception: The catalogue describes early Gellone ownership and use; no wider Frankish or Roman adoption is inferred.
stages.scope: BnF Latin 12048's principal late eighth-century sacramentary state; later marginal and f. 1 additions excluded from the coordinate.
stages.summary: The BnF description dates the codex to the last quarter of the eighth century and describes a Frankish Gelasian sacramentary containing Frankish, Roman and Gregorian liturgical material, plus later additions.
stages.witness_label: Paris BnF Latin 12048, Gellone Sacramentary

stages.date_label: manuscript copied at the turn of the eighth and ninth centuries (ELMSS 796–824; e-codices 'around 800')

evidence.claim: Images show the incipit, the Canon with the Remedius commemoration keyed to the Te igitur, and St Gall Masses in another hand; the record places the book at St Gall by about 850.
evidence.locus: pp. 32, 368 and 10; IIIF metadata; Scherrer 1875 p. 122 (TEI)

evidence.claim: Dates the copying 796–824, places it probably at Chur, calls the Remedius entry contemporary, and reports correction throughout at St Gall in the second half of the ninth century.
evidence.locus: Date; Origin and Provenance; Script Commentary

stages.label: St Gall 348 (Remedius) Gelasian sacramentary
stages.limitations: The 796–824 range dates the principal copy, not the composition of its prayers or a Frankish Gelasian archetype. The St Gall Masses and corrections are later, undated layers here, and no prayer-level comparison with Gellone, Rheinau or the Old Gelasian is made. Its relationship to St Gall 350 is not asserted.
stages.reception: The Remedius commemoration ties the book to the church of Chur around 800; the St Gall Masses and corrections show later use at St Gall. No wider Frankish adoption is inferred.
stages.scope: The principal Rhaetian copy of St. Gallen, Stiftsbibliothek, Cod. Sang. 348, with its Canon; the front St Gall Masses, the Remedius commemoration and later St Gall corrections are distinguished as separate layers.
stages.summary: A Frankish Gelasian sacramentary titled as a liber sacramentorum anni circuli Romanae ecclesiae (p. 32), with the Roman Canon (p. 368). A contemporary red-capital entry at the foot of p. 368 commemorates Bishop Remedius of Chur; Masses for the vigil and feast of St Gall stand in another hand at the front (p. 10).
stages.witness_label: St. Gallen, Stiftsbibliothek, Cod. Sang. 348

stages.date_label: early ninth century; precise copying date disputed

evidence.claim: Identifies the actual Cambrai codex and explicitly separates its reported 812–813 copying from the proposed earlier exemplar.

stages.label: Cambrai Hadrianum sacramentary copy
stages.limitations: No year coordinate is assigned while the competing 811/812, 812/813 and later palaeographic datings remain unresolved. The Roman exemplar sent to Charlemagne is not this extant codex; neither its date nor papal composition is assigned to the copy. Wilson 1915 and Lietzmann 1921 are modern editions.
stages.reception: A Frankish copy of a Gregorian sacramentary state; not proof of immediate universal replacement of Gelasian books.
stages.scope: Cambrai MS 164 (159), an extant Hadrianum-family sacramentary, with copy date deliberately unpositioned pending resolution of catalogue disagreement.
stages.summary: USUARIUM identifies the codex and lists Ordinary, Canon and Mass-prayer material. Its 812–813 copy assertion is different from its proposed 790–800 Aachen master-copy date; the wider inventory records competing datings.
stages.witness_label: Cambrai Bibliothèque municipale MS 164 (159)

evidence.claim: Identifies the manuscript and its indexed Ordinary, Canon and prayer sequence.

stages.label: Trento Gregorian sacramentary witness
stages.limitations: The 800–850 range dates the witness. The catalogue's Salzburg-model note is not an inspected exemplar or direction of borrowing. The 1985 critical edition is not a ninth-century reform, and the supplement has not been collated separately.
stages.reception: Local manuscript attestation only; no general Roman or Frankish adoption date established.
stages.scope: Trento cod. 1590 as an extant Gregorian sacramentary witness, with its supplement distinguished from the principal book.
stages.summary: The catalogue dates the manuscript to the first half of the ninth century and indexes a Mass Ordinary, Canon and annual prayers.

evidence.claim: Identifies the manuscript, Mass and Canon contents, and the distinct appendix and correction notices.

stages.reception: Manuscript witness with later Verona association; no inferred universal Roman use.
stages.scope: Padua Cathedral MS D. 47's principal Gregorian sacramentary state, with corrector and later Verona appendix left undated.

stages.scope: BnF Latin 13246's principal sacramentary text, with inserted and added material distinguished.

The 1917 facsimile plates show that the inserted Mass is a Mass for the ruler ('principem nostrum') in a different hand, and that f. 253v carries later cursive additions.

evidence.claim: Identifies ff. 12–67, approximate core date and later additions.

stages.limitations: The narrower 780–820 ELMSS estimate concerns the core, whereas the aggregate inventory gives eighth–ninth centuries. The Máel Caích hand is now image-checked at its f. 37r signature, but the extent and date of that revision remain undetermined and uncollated. Warner 1906/1915 are facsimile and edition dates, not early liturgical dates; no universal Celtic rite is inferred.
stages.reception: An Irish manuscript witness with later Lorrha associations; no all-Ireland or modern Catholic authorization claim.

stages.limitations: The title's declared audience is not a dated use record for a particular monastery, nor approval or reception in Lungro or Piana. No whole copy or exact predecessor has been inspected; its textual distinctness from 1683 remains unestablished.
stages.reception: The printing itself declares the Grottaferrata monastic use it serves; no broader territorial use is inferred.
stages.scope: Printing expressly for the Italo-Greek Basilian monks following the Grottaferrata Typikon, with the three named Eucharistic liturgies.

stages.date_label: Colophon: 28 February 1509; actual printing most likely 1519 by bibliographic analysis

evidence.claim: Original title identifies an Évora-custom missal; the colophon literally gives 28 February 1509; the inspected last leaf includes a local Mass formulary.

A later archdiocesan rule requires sufficient missals of Évora custom, establishing a jurisdictional use mandate without naming this exact printing or creating a new textual state.
evidence.locus: Title XXVII chapter I, fol. lxxv recto–verso, PDF pp. 169–170

stages.label: Printed Missale secundum consuetudinem Elborensis ecclesie
stages.limitations: The stage uses the bibliographically favored 1519 printing year; the original colophon literally says 1509 and remains a separate source datum. This is one printing event, not years of liturgical validity. Its prayers, rubrics, complete extent and relation to any predecessor remain uncollated. No authorization, adoption day or post-1570 continuation is inferred from the printed witness.
stages.reception: The distinct 1565 constitutions mandate missals of Évora custom across archdiocesan churches. They do not show that this exact BNP printing was used in each church or that the use continued after 1570.
stages.scope: An identifiable printed Évora-use Mass book, with title and one local votive formulary leaf inspected; no complete book recension or dated reform established.
stages.summary: The original title expressly names the Évora church's custom; its colophon prints 28 February 1509. The apparent discrepancy with printer chronology makes 1519 the most likely production year in the checked bibliographic study. This is a book-state attestation, not a claim that a reform took effect in either year.
stages.witness_label: BNP RES.155 A printed Évora missal

evidence.claim: The book names Évreux, the bishop's authority with chapter consent, Paris, 1740 and the royal privilege.
The mandate describes its editorial programme and recipients and is dated 18 April 1740.
evidence.locus: views 7–10, printed pp. [3]–6, complete mandate; dateline view 10

evidence.claim: Marginal source sigla, a movable-feast table, a notated Advent preface and the Canon opening are present at these inspected loci; no complete wording is imported.
evidence.locus: view 11 Monitum; view 12 movable-feast table; view 280 printed p. 212; view 315 printed p. 245

stages.label: 1740 Évreux diocesan missal
stages.limitations: The mandate describes changes relative to earlier practice, but no predecessor Évreux missal has been collated; no substantive transition, whole-book text or physical completeness is claimed. Printing year and mandate date are distinct events.
stages.reception: The mandate names diocesan churches, chapters, orders, colleges, monasteries, communities and confraternities, then priests bound by law or custom to the Évreux Office, and forbids other missals. This records the stated command and recipients, not actual uptake, a first effective date or later replacement.
stages.scope: The identified 1740 Évreux missal, its complete episcopal mandate, and selected original preface and Canon loci.
stages.summary: The title names Bishop Pierre-Jules-César de Rochechouart and the cathedral chapter. His mandate, dated 18 April 1740, says the editors went back to the Ordo Romanus and ancient sacramentaries, drew many Secrets and Postcommunions from the recently edited Leonine Sacramentary, added prefaces for Advent, Corpus Christi and some feasts, took sung texts from Scripture, restricted sequences to solemn days, arranged ceremonies after the older Évreux form, and restored proper ferial epistles and gospels. It commands the diocese's churches, chapters, orders, colleges, monasteries, communities, confraternities and priests bound by law or custom to the Évreux Office to use this missal and no other.
stages.witness_label: Missale Ebroicense, Paris 1740, Lyon SJ LB 030/80

evidence.claim: The book names Lodève, the bishop's authority with chapter consent, Paris, 1776 and the royal privilege.
The letter states the adoption and adaptation of the Paris Missal and is dated 10 September 1775.
evidence.locus: views 9–12, printed pp. 5–8; account of adoption view 11; mandate, dateline and Monitum view 12

evidence.claim: The Canon opens at this inspected page with a marginal Roman-sacramentary siglum.

stages.label: 1776 Lodève diocesan missal (Paris missal adopted with local adaptation)
stages.limitations: The letter's account of what was adopted and adapted is a primary description; no Paris missal or earlier Lodève missal has been collated with this book, so no transition is recorded. The 1775 letter and the 1776 printing are distinct events.
stages.reception: The mandate is addressed to the diocese's churches and rectors, orders, colleges, monasteries, communities and priests bound to the Lodève Office and forbids other missals. Actual uptake and duration of use are not established.
stages.scope: The identified 1776 Lodève missal, its complete pastoral letter and the Canon opening.
stages.summary: The letter of Bishop Jean-Félix-Henri de Fumel says the old Lodève breviary had recently been restored, that only one copy of the old Lodève missal survived, and that, given the agreement found between the old Lodève and Paris breviaries, and presumed ('praesumpta') between the old missals of both churches, the Paris Missal was adopted ('Missale Parisiense duximus adoptandum'), with items removed from or added to the Proper of Time and the Proper and Common of Saints to suit Lodève practice and the rubrics adapted to local use. Proper Masses and prefaces are given to the solemnities and patronal feasts. The mandate commands diocesan churches, orders, colleges, monasteries, communities and priests bound to the Lodève Office to use this missal and no other.
stages.witness_label: Missale Lodovense, Paris 1776, Lyon 31754

stages.date_label: 1543 colophon (Lyon printing for a Le Puy bookseller)

evidence.claim: The book is titled a missal for the use of the church of Le Puy, sold at Le Puy by Jean Allard.
Printed at Lyon by Theobaldus Paganus for Jean Allard of Le Puy, 1543.
evidence.locus: view 673, f. CCCXII, colophon and register

evidence.claim: The Canon from Te igitur to Communicantes is present on this inspected page.

stages.label: 1543 Le Puy diocesan missal
stages.limitations: No episcopal authority, calendar or proper sections were inspected; the commercial publication does not by itself establish episcopal approval. No predecessor or successor collation, transition or complete text is claimed; the observed Canon wording is not a collated variant claim.
stages.reception: Sale at Le Puy and the title's 'ad usum Aniciensis ecclesiae' attest intended local use, not actual adoption, approval or duration of use.
stages.scope: The identified 1543 Le Puy missal at its title, Canon and colophon.
stages.summary: A pre-Tridentine printing for the use of the church of Le Puy. The title promises chant and notes and newly added Masses; the colophon on f. CCCXII says Thibaud Payen printed it at Lyon in 1543 at the cost of Jean Allard, bookseller of Le Puy. The Canon is present; its opening reads 'pro nostris delictis et pro ecclesia' and names the bishop and king, observed here without collation.
stages.witness_label: Missale ad usum Aniciensis ecclesiae, Lyon 1543, Lyon Rés 129080

evidence.claim: The book names Autun, the bishop's authority with chapter consent and 1831.
The mandate describes the revision and is dated 30 December 1830, with use required six months later.

evidence.claim: The Canon opens at this inspected page.

stages.label: 1831 Autun diocesan missal
stages.limitations: The mandate's account is a primary description; neither the predecessor breviary nor an earlier missal has been collated. The mandate date, the six-month term and the printing year are distinct events; no transition or complete text is claimed.
stages.reception: The mandate is addressed to the churches, rectors, confraternities, communities and priests bound to the Autun Office. Actual uptake is not established; the 1856 return to the Roman liturgy (next stage) shows the book was later superseded.
stages.scope: The identified 1831 Autun missal, its episcopal mandate and the Canon opening.
stages.summary: The mandate of Bishop du Trousset d'Héricourt says that his predecessor's new breviary required a matching missal; the work, begun earlier and interrupted by death, reached him with errors and was completed by experts who conformed the missal to the general rubrics and the breviary, raised some Masses in rank, restored some and introduced new ones, and increased the cult of the Virgin, the Apostles and the bishops of Autun, Chalon and Mâcon. It orders the churches, rectors, confraternities, communities and priests bound to the Autun Office to use this missal, and no other, six months after the mandate's date.
stages.witness_label: Missale Aeduense, Autun 1831, Lyon copy (Google Books RxTk440szmAC)

stages.date_label: 1858 printing; SRC decree of 17 April 1856 approving the calendar and proper; mandate of 11 May 1856

evidence.claim: Proper Masses of the church of Autun approved by Pius IX and published by order of Bishop de Marguerye, Autun, 1858.
The mandate prescribes the Roman Missal and other Roman books with the approved Autun propers and is dated 11 May 1856.
evidence.locus: PA1, printed p. 1, mandate and dateline

evidence.claim: The SRC letter of 28 February 1856 grants privileges for the resumption of the Roman liturgy at Autun, and the SRC decree of 17 April 1856 approves the perpetual calendar and proper of Offices and Masses; both carry the concordat of 11 May 1856.
The bishop certifies on 1 September 1858 that the printed proper agrees with the approved original.
evidence.locus: PA5-IA1, certification heading (body read by OCR)

stages.label: 1858 Autun proper Masses for the restored Roman liturgy
stages.limitations: The Mass formularies were not examined individually and the Roman Missal edition used is not identified. The 1856 mandate left the effective day to a later announcement; no effective date is asserted. No transition from the 1831 missal is recorded because no Roman Missal text is in evidence here.
stages.reception: The mandate binds all clergy of the diocese from a day to be announced. The announcement and actual implementation are not established.
stages.scope: The identified 1858 Autun proper of Masses, its bishop's mandate restoring the Roman liturgy, the SRC letter and the printer's certification.
stages.summary: Bishop Frédéric de Marguerye's mandate of 11 May 1856 says that proper Masses and Offices of the three old dioceses of Autun, Chalon and Mâcon were composed according to the Roman rite with a calendar, examined by the Congregation of Rites and approved by Pius IX as a Roman-Autun calendar with proper Offices and Masses. It orders all clergy, from a day to be announced, to use only the Ritual, Ceremonial, Breviary and Missal of the Roman Church together with these approved propers, observing the Congregation's rubrics and decrees. Printed p. 3 carries two SRC acts, each with the bishop's concordat of 11 May 1856: a letter of 28 February 1856 granting privileges asked for the prompt resumption of the Roman liturgy in the diocese (among them continuing the custom of three consecutive Christmas night Masses), and the decree of 17 April 1856 approving the perpetual calendar and the proper of Offices and Masses, with the corrections noted, for perpetual observance in the Hours and in Masses. A certification dated 1 September 1858 attests that the printed proper agrees with the approved original.
stages.witness_label: Missae ecclesiae Aeduensi propriae, Autun 1858, Lyon copy (Google Books hp2fFDt6djwC)

evidence.claim: The book names Chalon, the bishop's authority with chapter consent, Paris, 1765 and the royal privilege.

evidence.claim: The book names Couserans, the bishop's order and authority with chapter consent, Paris, 1753 and the royal privilege.

The Canon opens at this inspected page.

stages.label: 1753 Couserans diocesan missal
stages.limitations: The letter's account is a primary description; no predecessor book or Roman Missal has been collated and no transition is claimed.

stages.scope: The identified 1753 Couserans missal, its complete letter and mandate, and the Canon opening.
stages.summary: Bishop Joseph de Saint-André Marnais de Verceil's letter says the recently issued breviary required a matching missal. As his predecessor took antiphons and responsories of the breviary from Scripture, so the introits, graduals, offertories and communions of the missal are taken from Scripture. Nothing belonging to the norm of the Sacrifice observed in the whole Latin Church was changed, nothing new was introduced in the rites, and only a very few formerly frequent local usages were restored, keeping those customary to the diocese's priests and used by the Roman Church. All priests of the diocese are to use the new missal in private and solemn Masses and no other, except the Roman Missal in private Masses.
stages.witness_label: Missale Conseranense, Paris 1753, BU Toulouse Res 1335

evidence.claim: The book names Albi, the archbishop's authority with chapter consent, Paris, 1766 and the royal privilege.

stages.label: 1766 Albi diocesan missal
stages.limitations: The letter's account is a primary description; no predecessor missal is collated and no transition is claimed. The 1763 letter, the 1764 catalogue record and this 1766 printing are distinct; whether 1766 reprints a 1764 first printing is unresolved.

stages.summary: Archbishop Léopold-Charles de Choiseul's letter says prefaces were added where proper ones were lacking (Advent, Corpus Christi, Dedication, All Saints and others), following the ancient Roman custom still kept in the Ambrosian rite; most collects, secrets and postcommunions were taken from ancient sacramentaries, including the Leonine Sacramentary published at the Vatican under Clement XII, with very few new prayers modelled on them, and slight verbal changes were allowed without altering doctrine. The mandate orders the churches, deans, rectors, orders, colleges, monasteries, communities and priests bound to the Albi Office to use this missal and no other, and forbids printers to reprint the old missals.
stages.witness_label: Missale Albiense, Paris 1766, BU Toulouse Res 1341

evidence.claim: The volume titled 'Bajocensis' is the Bayonne missal printed by order of Étienne Poncher, finished in January 1544 new style (28 January, and 24 January in Marais's quoted conclusion); Mazarine 1162 B is the only known copy.
Transcribed title, printer and date, and physical description.
Contents: calendar, temporale incipit for the diocese of Bayonne, notated prefaces, Canon with additions, sanctoral, common and votive Masses.

stages.label: 1543/1544 Bayonne diocesan missal of Bishop Étienne Poncher
stages.limitations: Documented from an inspected scholarly description with exact loci, not from the original; Dubarat's characterization of the Canon additions as Gallican is his judgment. No collation, transition or complete text is claimed.
stages.reception: The title states episcopal order for the cathedral church of Bayonne. Actual diocesan use and duration are not established.
stages.scope: The 1543/1544 Bayonne missal as described by Dubarat from the Mazarine copy: title, physical make-up, calendar, temporale, Ordinary with notated prefaces, Canon and sanctoral.
stages.summary: Dubarat, following P. Marais, restores to Bayonne a Paris missal of 1543 (finished in January 1544 new style; he gives both 28 and 24 January) whose title misprints 'Bajocensis' for Bayonne: folio 1 reads 'secundum usum ecclesie diocesis Bajon.', the arms and order are those of Étienne Poncher, bishop of Bayonne, and the title calls the book carefully emended, enlarged and revised. He describes a calendar, blessings including one for ships, a temporale for the diocese of Bayonne, notated prefaces including a proper Palm Sunday preface, a Canon with added passages, and a sanctoral, common and votive Masses in a second part.

stages.date_label: Missal of 1614 with its mandate, as described and quoted by Du Lac

evidence.claim: The 1607/1614 books reproduce the Roman books; the 1614 missal mandate is quoted; the 1667 reissue kept the missal Roman.

stages.label: 1614 Amiens missal conformed to the Roman Missal (La Marthonie)
stages.limitations: The original was not inspected; the catalogue witness is linked by title and year only. Du Lac is a polemical 1849 survey. No collation with the Roman Missal is claimed, and the 1667 reissue is not a separate stage here.
stages.reception: The mandate's addressees and the actual uptake are not given by Du Lac.
stages.scope: Du Lac's description of the 1614 Amiens missal and the sentence he quotes from its mandate.
stages.summary: Du Lac says the two editions of the Amiens books after the reform of Pius V began under Bishop de La Marthonie with the breviary of 1607 and the missal of 1614, which practically reproduced the Roman books. He quotes the missal's mandate: the missal was emended so that, apart from the offices of the saints proper to the diocese, the clergy would recognize the Roman. He adds that Bishop Faure's reissue of 1667 made some changes but that the missal stayed wholly faithful to the Roman.
stages.witness_label: Amiens missal of 1614 (Bishop Geoffroy de La Marthonie); catalogue witness Missale ad usum insignis Ecclesiae Ambianensis, 1614

stages.date_label: Missal of 1752, as dated by Du Lac

stages.label: 1752 Amiens missal of Bishop d'Orléans de La Motte
stages.limitations: The original was not inspected; the catalogue witness is linked by title and year only. No mandate date, contents list or collation is available; no transition from 1614 is claimed because no component is described at both ends.
stages.reception: Du Lac (p. 393) reports La Motte's statement that the new liturgy was introduced with great difficulty; actual uptake is not established. Du Lac says the diocese lived on this basis until the second breviary edition of 1840.
stages.scope: Du Lac's description of the 1752 Amiens missal published to accompany the 1746 breviary.
stages.summary: Du Lac says that Bishop d'Orléans de La Motte, after publishing the Amiens breviary in 1746, issued in 1752 a missal in harmony with it, and that from this time the church of Amiens abandoned its Roman-French usages: the 1746 breviary and the 1752 missal were composed on the model of the new books then in fashion. He names one borrowing, the All Saints preface 'Quos imitatione sequi non possumus' from the Troyes missal.
stages.witness_label: Missale Ambianensis Ecclesiae, 1752 (catalogue witness)

The earlier change away from the Roman books is dated only approximately.

stages.scope: A reported diocesan restoration of the Roman liturgy.

stages.date_label: Paris 1753 printing; archiepiscopal mandate dated 18 November 1752 (as described by Dubarat)

evidence.claim: Mandate of 18 November 1752 quoted on the missal's relation to the breviary, the unchanged order of Mass, local rites and the sources of chants and orations.
Title, imprint (Paris, Garnier and Le Prieur, 1753) and contents of the Missale Auscitanum; Lebeuf's chant for the 1755 Antiphonarium and Graduale.

stages.label: 1753 Missale Auscitanum of Archbishop de Montillet
stages.limitations: A scholarly description; the original was not inspected and the catalogue witness is linked by title and year only. No collation; the mandate's date and the printing year are distinct events.
stages.reception: Dubarat (p. cliv) says that of the province, Auch, Couserans, Comminges and Bayonne took the new Auch breviary, and that the chapter's opposition was overcome by gifts of the new books; uptake of the missal is not separately established.
stages.scope: Dubarat's transcription of the title and his description of contents, with the historical part of the mandate that he quotes.
stages.summary: Dubarat transcribes the title (Missale Auscitanum, issued by the authority of Archbishop Jean-François de Montillet with chapter consent, Paris, Garnier and Le Prieur, 1753) and lists the contents: mandate, rubrics, Proper of Time from Advent, Ordo missae at p. 211, Proper of Saints, Common, Passions with chant and a Mass of the Sacred Heart. From the mandate dated 18 November 1752 he quotes that the missal answers the restored Auch breviary; that everything belonging to the order of Mass and the consecration was kept unchanged; that local rites were retained, a very few being introduced or renewed from ancient Auch usage, such as a prophecy before the Epistle at Christmas and Epiphany; that the sung parts were composed from Scripture; and that the collects, secrets and postcommunions were taken from the oldest sacramentaries, the Roman especially. The chant books of 1755 record that Jean Lebeuf composed their chant at Paris in 1753–1755.
stages.witness_label: Missale Auscitanum, Paris, J.-B. Garnier and P.-A. Le Prieur, 1753 (described by Dubarat; catalogue witness linked by title and year)

stages.label: 1753 Missale Baionense of Bishop d'Arche (Auch missal adopted)
stages.limitations: A scholarly description; the original was not inspected and the catalogue witness is linked by title and year only. Dubarat's preface list on p. clxxvii includes prefaces of St John the Baptist and of the Saints, while p. ccxxviii says the 1836 edition has those prefaces and the d'Arche missal lacks them; the list may mix editions (it notes a Sacred Heart preface added about 1770). The stage records the Bayonne printing by which d'Arche received the missal of the Auch province, accommodated to Bayonne use: it is a reception of the Auch missal (french-dioceses-a-batch4:auch-1753), not evidence of an independent Bayonne text state, and no reception transition is recorded.
stages.reception: Reception of the Auch missal: the mandate adopts the missal of the Auch province accommodated to Bayonne use and forbids any other (p. clxxvii). The Bayonne bureau's deliberation of 10 April 1753 recalls an agreement of 4 February 1751 to take 300 copies of the proper Missal (p. cliv); actual use is not established.
stages.scope: Dubarat's account of the adoption, his quotation of the mandate and his physical description of the missal.
stages.summary: Dubarat says that Bishop Guillaume d'Arche adopted the Auch missal together with the Auch breviary and published it in 1753 as the Missale Baionense, regulated by the breviary. He quotes the mandate dated at Bayonne on the sixth kalends of June 1753, which, having lately adopted the Auch breviary, adopts the missal of the same province and commands every church and priest of the diocese to use this Auch missal accommodated to Bayonne and no other. He notes the changed Sunday introits, the deacon's chanting of the genealogies at Christmas and Epiphany after the ninth respond, the prostration at the Passion, many prefaces and many sequences. His bibliography describes the folio volume, its imprint given as 'Parisiis etc., comme au missel d'Auch': mandate, movable feasts, rubrics and preparation prayers, blessings, Proper of Time and of Saints, Common, Proses and notated Passions, with a frontispiece. A further undated entry ('Item', a fine edition with fourteen engravings, among them Christ on the Cross at the Canon and a Sacred Heart) may describe another edition and is not attributed to 1753 here.
stages.witness_label: Missale Baionense of Guillaume d'Arche, Paris, 1753 (described by Dubarat; catalogue witness linked by title and year)

Dubarat's title transcription calls the book 'denuo typis mandatum' (printed again) and it carries d'Arche's mandate; its distinctness from the 1753 book rests only on his statement about the two prefaces, which p. clxxvii contradicts, so it may be a witness of the same state.

Brun in 1836, and describes it: d'Arche's mandate at the head, rubrics, Propers and Commons, with the prefaces of St John the Baptist and of the Saints, which he says are not in the d'Arche missal, and engravings. He adds that the Auch missal, antiphonary and vesperal are the same as Bayonne's under d'Arbou and Lacroix, apart from title and small local differences. Earlier, Bishop d'Astros had restored the Auch breviary at Bayonne by an ordinance of 25 September 1827.

stages.label: 1774 Toulouse missal (Loménie de Brienne)
stages.limitations: The letter's account of change is a contemporary claim; no predecessor missal was collated. The 1772 letter date and the 1774 title date are distinct events. Whether this copy belongs to the same printing as the catalogue's 1773 entry is unresolved.
stages.reception: The letter commands all churches, chapters, monasteries, convents, seminaries, colleges, communities and orders of the diocese, and priests bound by law or custom to the Toulouse Office, to use this missal and forbids others. The printed command names its addressees; it does not establish uniform actual uptake, a first effective-use date or the duration of use.
stages.scope: One identified 1774 printing, its title and the archbishop's complete pastoral letter describing the edition's programme.
stages.summary: The title names Archbishop Étienne-Charles de Loménie de Brienne's authority with chapter consent. His letter says the new missal was made to agree with his recently published breviary (same Gospels, collects and scriptural chant texts) while keeping the Latin rite and order. It describes the distribution of Gospel and Epistle readings, with at least three ferial Gospels each week (Monday, Wednesday and Friday), each paired with its own Epistle. It says that the old Toulouse missal already gave proper Gospels to Advent ferias except Saturday. Chant texts were largely adopted from French missals, especially the Paris missal. Most orations came from the ancient sacramentaries. Prefaces were added for Advent, Septuagesima, saints, Corpus Christi, the Dedication and Toulouse saints, with two prefaces for Stephen and Saturninus taken from the old Missale Gothicum. Old sequences were kept for Easter, Pentecost, Christmas and Corpus Christi, and the rest came from the Paris missal. A Mass for the King was added. The letter commands all churches, chapters, monasteries, convents, seminaries, colleges, communities, orders and priests bound to the Toulouse Office to use this missal and forbids others.

stages.scope: A Roman-Missal state: a Roman Missal with a printed Soissons proper bound after it, as described by Leclercq de Laprairie.
stages.summary: Leclercq de Laprairie describes a Roman Missal at the church of Acy followed by a 'Proprium Missalis Suessionensis' printed at Soissons by Hanisset with permission in 1687, during a vacancy of the see; the seminary library had another copy. stages.date_label: Title dated 1745; episcopal letter dated Soissons, 6 January 1745

evidence.claim: Missale Suessionense by Fitz-James's authority with chapter consent; Paris, J.-B. Coignard, 1745, royal privilege.
Primary description: prior forced use of the Roman Missal for want of Soissons copies; scriptural composition; Wednesday/Friday lessons; sacramentary orations; added prefaces; restored rites.
Mandate to the named institutions and priests; prohibition of other missals and rites; dated Soissons, 6 January 1745.

stages.label: 1745 Soissons missal (Fitz-James)
stages.limitations: The letter's comparison with earlier practice is a contemporary claim; no earlier Soissons missal or Roman Missal was collated. The post-Tridentine Soissons edition it mentions is unidentified.
stages.reception: The letter commands all churches, chapters, pastors, monasteries, colleges, communities, sodalities and priests bound to the Soissons Office. The printed command names its addressees; it does not establish uniform actual uptake, a first effective-use date or the duration of use.
stages.scope: One identified 1745 printing, its title and the bishop's complete letter describing the edition.
stages.summary: Bishop François de Fitz-James issues the missal after his new breviary. He says that copies of the Soissons missal hardly survived, so almost all churches had been forced to use the Roman Missal, and that Soissons rites survived only orally and were mixed with Roman ones. Apart from the orations, the body of the missal is composed from Scripture. Proper Epistles and Gospels for Wednesdays and Fridays are presented as an old Soissons usage, found in older Soissons missals including one printed shortly after Trent. The Gospels are distributed so that all four evangelists are read in a year. Orations come mostly from ancient sacramentaries, and a few prefaces were added (for example Advent and principal feasts). Lapsed rites common to neighbouring churches of the Reims province were restored, following Sixtus V's principle. All churches, chapters, pastors, monasteries, colleges, communities, sodalities and priests bound to the Soissons Office must use this missal; other missals and rites are forbidden.
stages.witness_label: Missale Suessionense, Paris 1745, BM Lyon SJ LB 030/68 (Numelyo; Google Books JWXbxJ1ccrQC)

stages.limitations: The letter was not viewed; its content is reported by a polemical survey. stages.reception: The letter addresses the clergy of the whole province with the suffragans' consent; actual uptake in Grenoble, Valence, Viviers and Die is not established.

stages.summary: The 1849 survey describes Archbishop Lefranc de Pompignan's pastoral letter of 18 August 1782. It is addressed to the clergy of Vienne and, with the comprovincial bishops' consent, to the clergy of each diocese of the province, and it promulgates the new missal and breviary together. The author says Pompignan replaced the earlier Villars liturgy by adopting the Paris books of Vintimille, Viger and Mésenguy with some cuts, additions and corrections, after the provincial assembly of 1775. Pompignan's 1903 biographer notes that the breviary and missal were published in 1783 at Grenoble by the widow Giroud, with a Latin preface on the wish for books common to the province.

stages.summary: Lalore prints Bishop Jacques-Bénigne Bossuet's Latin mandate of 16 September 1735 and his French mandate of 26 September 1736. Lalore's chronology records a royal commission under Cardinal de Rohan, a Conseil d'État arrêt of 11 June 1737, and Bossuet's fourth pastoral instruction and ordinance of 15 October 1738, in which he retracted several provisions of the missal and restored the former rubrics on three principal points (pp. 112, 117).

Boucarut (1857) says the breviary and missal were given by Bishop de Chaffoy in 1826, adapted from the Besançon books, that the 1835 synod ordered Mass to be said according to the Missale Nemausense, and that the missal differed from the Roman only in its sung parts and some epistles, gospels and orations, keeping the Roman order, Canon and Ordinary.

He orders all churches, monasteries, colleges and priests of the diocese to use it in solemn and private Masses and no other. The letter is dated at Pamiers on 1 June 1781.

stages.reception: The book is titled for the abbey and order of Saint-Ruf; use in its dependent priories is not established.
stages.scope: One identified printing: subscription, physical make-up and Chevalier's description of its ceremonial content.
stages.summary: Chevalier transcribes the subscription on the recto of the last leaf: the missal for the use of the abbey of Saint-Ruf, ordered and completed, was printed in Valence by Jean Belon and Pierre de Mole, partners, on the last day of April 1508; Belon's mark follows. He describes a quarto in red and black in three parts: 184 numbered leaves, an unnumbered 14-leaf Canon in very large type, and 120 leaves. He says the missal also contains, spread through its parts, the ceremonial proper to the abbey, drawn from the Ordinarium of G. de Nemauso, that of Abbot Lethbert and customs confirmed by general chapters.
